Revisiting the Fermionic Dark Matter Absorption on Electron Target

Abstract

We perform a systematic study of the fermionic DM absorption interactions on electron target in the context of effective field theory. The fermionic DM absorption is not just sensitive to sub-MeV DM with efficient energy release, but also gives a unique signature with clear peak in the electron recoil spectrum whose shape is largely determined by the atomic effects. Fitting with the Xenon1T and PandaX-II data prefers DM mass at mχ=59m_{\chi}=59 keV and 105 keV, respectively, while the cut-off scale is probed up to around 1 TeV. The DM overproduction in the early Universe, the invisible decay effect on the cosmological evolution, and the astrophysical X(gamma)-ray from the DM visible decays are thoroughly explored to give up-to-date constraints. With stringent bounds on the tensor and pseudo-scalar operators, the other fermionic DM operators are of particular interest at tonne-scale direct detection experiments such as PandaX-4T, XENONnT, and LZ.

I Introduction

The nature of dark matter (DM) remains a mysterious puzzle in our understanding of the Universe [1, 2]. The possible particle characteristic of DM is a well-motivated scenario to be probed by the direct detection experiments [3, 4] and indirect observations [5, 6]. The stability of DM particle is usually realized by some discrete symmetry such as ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} [7, 8, 9]. A direct consequence is that in direct detection, the scattering process has a DM particle in the initial state and another DM particle in the final one. The energy deposit comes from the DM kinetic energy. With typical experimental threshold at 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1) keV, direct detection experiments are only sensitive to the DM mass above GeV. In the GeV∼\simTeV mass range, the null result from the direct detection experiments has put very strong limit on the DM interaction strength with the Standard Model (SM) particles [10, 11]. In contrast, the cross section of sub-GeV light DM scattering with SM particles is much less stringently constrained and can still be large [3, 4]. More attention has been turned to light DM alternatives with sub-GeV mass [12] or even lighter ones such as the sterile neutrino DM [13, 14, 15, 16].

However, one difficulty for the light DM detection is its small recoil energy. For a typical DM scattering with nuclei target, the recoil energy Tr=4​mχ​mA​Tχ/(mχ+mA)2T_{r}=4m_{\chi}m_{A}T_{\chi}/(m_{\chi}+m_{A})^{2} is proportionally scaled from the DM kinetic energy TχT_{\chi}. The most efficient energy transfer happens when the DM mass mχm_{\chi} is roughly the size of the atomic mass mAm_{A} of the nuclei target, Tr≈TχT_{r}\approx T_{\chi}. With light DM, mχ≪mAm_{\chi}\ll m_{A}, the recoil energy Tr≈4​mχ​Tχ/mAT_{r}\approx 4m_{\chi}T_{\chi}/m_{A} decreases with not just the DM mass mχm_{\chi} but also its kinetic energy TχT_{\chi}. More importantly, the DM kinetic energy is also proportional to its mass, Tχ≈12​mχ​vχ2T_{\chi}\approx\frac{1}{2}m_{\chi}v^{2}_{\chi}, while the distribution of its velocity vχv_{\chi} is fixed by the galaxy gravitational potential [17]. Altogether, the nuclear recoil from the light DM scattering scales with mχ2m^{2}_{\chi}. This explains why the direction detection sensitivity deteriorate fast in the sub-GeV range. It is desirable to find possible ways to overcome this difficulty.

There are several ways of improving the detection of light DM. For nuclear recoil, the detection threshold can be lowered by using Germanium point-contact detector [18], bolometer [20, 19], nuclear bremsstrahlung [21, 22], and Migdal effect [23, 24, 25, 30, 22, 33, 32, 31, 29, 28, 27, 26]. Or one may replace the nuclear recoil by electron recoil. Then, the elastic recoil energy is Tr=4​mχ​me​Tχ/(mχ+me)2T_{r}=4m_{\chi}m_{e}T_{\chi}/(m_{\chi}+m_{e})^{2} which removes the suppression factor mχ/mAm_{\chi}/m_{A}. In addition to using the conventional detector for measuring the electron recoils, various new technology has been developed. From the condensed matter side, the typically small energy gap is of great advantage to build a low threshold detector such as using superheated liquid [34], super-conduction [35], Fermi degenerate materials [36], super-fluid [37], scintillation [38], magnetic molecular [39], Dirac material [40], diamond crystal [41], nanowire [42], nanotube [43], magnon [44], graphene [45], and plasmon [46]. In particular, a semi-conductor detector such as skipper CCD is very sensitive to single electron events [47]. The biological DNA also provides an interesting possibility [48].

On the other hand, DM particles upscattered to higher energy can also overcome the detection threshold. Several possibilities have been discussed in the literature. The nonrelativistic DM particles can be boosted by the cosmic rays to gain sufficient energy [49, 50, 51, 52, 53, 54, 57, 58, 61, 62, 64, 59, 60, 63, 56, 55]. This cosmic ray boosted DM (CRDM) scenario can happen as long as DM interacts with SM particles which is exactly the foundation of DM direct detection. Actual experimental search with real DM direct detection data has been carried out by PandaX-II [65] and CDEX [66], in addition to those constraints from neutrino experiments [51, 67, 68, 69, 70, 71] and indirect constraints [49, 72]. The CRDM may also be produced by astrophysical neutrinos [73, 74, 75, 76, 77, 78] and blazar [79]. If the DM particle is light enough, it is also possible for them to be produced by the cosmic ray interactions with the atmosphere [80, 81, 82]. Another place to boost light DM is the Sun [83, 84, 85, 87, 86, 88]. With multiple components, the boosted light DM can also happen inside the dark sector [89, 90, 91, 93, 92].

Another possibility is the fermionic DM absorption. The upscattered DM scenarios mentioned in the above paragraph can probe light DM, but the dependence on the DM mass may not be significant. This is because smaller mass usually means smaller effect on the kinematics, especially if DM particles are highly boosted. In order for DM detection to be sensitive to the light DM mass, the mass term should dominate the relevant kinematics. Namely, non-relativistic DM may have some advantage in this regard. If a nonrelativistic DM releases all its mass into energy, its mass is the dominant factor and the detection threshold can also be overcome with efficient amplification by the speed of light, E=m​c2E=mc^{2}. This is exactly the idea of DM absorption for bosonic [94, 95, 98, 96, 97, 99, 100, 101, 102] and fermionic [103, 104, 105] DM.

This paper is organized as follows. In Sec. II, we introduce the motivation for the sub-MeV fermionic absorption DM and enumerate all the possible effective absorption operators. In Sec. II.1 we discuss the signal in direct detection experiment. Then we evaluate the constraints from DM overproduction of the early Universe in Sec. III as well as the cosmological evolution constraint on the invisible decay χ→3​ν\chi\rightarrow 3\nu and astrophysical constraints with X(gamma)-rays on the visible decay modes χ→ν+γ⁡(s)\chi\rightarrow\nu+\gamma(s) in Sec. V. More details about the calculation of DM decay is provided in Sec. IV. Our main results are summarized in Sec. VI. On the technical side, we provide simplified algorithms for a general-purpose analytic χ2\chi^{2} fit with collective marginalization in App. A.

II Sub-MeV Fermionic Absorption DM on Electron Target

As pointed out above, the light DM has intrinsic difficulty in the direct detection experiments due to energy threshold. One possible way of overcoming this comes from the fermionic DM absorption, χ​e→ν​e\chi e\rightarrow\nu e, where the DM particle χ\chi scatters into a massless SM neutrino ν\nu. Placing neutrino in the final state not only conserves charge but also is the most economical choice to maximize the energy release. Then the DM mass mχm_{\chi} is wholy converted to the electron recoil and neutrino energies. The fermionic DM absorption on a nuclei target is also possible [103, 104] but requires heavier DM above MeV mass to overcome the detection threshold. In our current paper, we focus on the electron target that is optimal for sub-MeV DM [105].

For a free electron target at rest, the electron recoil energy is Tr≈mχ2/2​meT_{r}\approx m^{2}_{\chi}/2m_{e} [105], which is a good approximation for mχ≪mem_{\chi}\ll m_{e}. A keV scale DM can already produce large enough electron recoil energy to overcome the detection threshold that is typically 1 keV for the electron signal [106, 107]. Although larger electron recoil energy TrT_{r} is better for direct detection threshold, the DM mass is not larger the better. For mχ=1m_{\chi}=1 MeV, the electron recoil approaches 1 MeV which may saturate the detector capability. So we focus on the sub-MeV DM mass range with 1 keV≲mχ≲1\lesssim m_{\chi}\lesssim 1 MeV across this paper.

To make a systematic study of the fermionic DM absorption, we take the effective field theory (EFT) approach for a model independent analysis. As argued at the beginning of this section, the relevant degrees of freedom are the light SM particles, electron and neutrino, augmented with an additional DM particle. Usually, the SM gauge symmetries U​(1)Y×S​U​(2)L×S​U​(3)cU(1)_{Y}\times SU(2)_{L}\times SU(3)_{c} is kept intact for an EFT approach. Nevertheless, the DM direct detection happens at low energy where the electroweak part is broken. Only the electromagnetic U​(1)emU(1)_{\rm em} is a good symmetry to guide the construction of EFT operators as far as gauge symmetry of the theory is concerned. The strong interaction S​U​(3)cSU(3)_{c} is of no relevance since no color degrees of freedom are involved.

For the fermionic DM absorption on the electron target, the leading local interactions are dimension-six operators involving a dark matter particle χ\chi, an active SM neutrino ν\nu and an electron current,

𝒪e​ν​χS≡(e¯​e)​(ν¯L​χR),\displaystyle{\cal O}_{e\nu\chi}^{S}\equiv(\bar{e}e)(\bar{\nu}_{L}\chi_{R}), (1a)
𝒪e​ν​χP≡(e¯​i​γ5​e)​(ν¯L​χR),\displaystyle{\cal O}_{e\nu\chi}^{P}\equiv(\bar{e}i\gamma_{5}e)(\bar{\nu}_{L}\chi_{R}), (1b)
𝒪e​ν​χV≡(e¯​γμ​e)​(ν¯L​γμ​χL),\displaystyle{\cal O}_{e\nu\chi}^{V}\equiv(\bar{e}\gamma_{\mu}e)(\bar{\nu}_{L}\gamma^{\mu}\chi_{L}), (1c)
𝒪e​ν​χA≡(e¯​γμ​γ5​e)​(ν¯L​γμ​χL),\displaystyle{\cal O}_{e\nu\chi}^{A}\equiv(\bar{e}\gamma_{\mu}\gamma_{5}e)(\bar{\nu}_{L}\gamma^{\mu}\chi_{L}), (1d)
𝒪e​ν​χT≡(e¯​σμ​ν​e)​(ν¯L​σμ​ν​χR),\displaystyle{\cal O}_{e\nu\chi}^{T}\equiv(\bar{e}\sigma_{\mu\nu}e)(\bar{\nu}_{L}\sigma^{\mu\nu}\chi_{R}), (1e)

and their Hermitian conjugates. For completeness, we have considered all the five independent Lorentz structures for the electron bilinear (scalar [S], pseudo-scalar [P], vector [V], axial-vector [A] and tensor [T]). The neutrino field is taken to be the SM left-handed component νL\nu_{L} and the DM χ\chi is assumed to be a Dirac particle for convenience. Any other types of operators can be converted to those in (1) by Dirac gamma matrix identities and Fierz transformations [108, 109, 110]. For instance, the operator (e¯​σμ​ν​γ5​e)​(ν¯L​σμ​ν​χR)(\bar{e}\sigma_{\mu\nu}\gamma_{5}e)(\bar{\nu}_{L}\sigma^{\mu\nu}\chi_{R}) is equivalent to 𝒪e​ν​χT{\cal O}_{e\nu\chi}^{T} by the identities σμ​ν​γ5=i2​ϵμ​ν​ρ​σ​σρ​σ\sigma^{\mu\nu}\gamma^{5}={i\over 2}\epsilon^{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}\sigma_{\rho\sigma} and γ5​PR=PR\gamma_{5}P_{R}=P_{R} with PRP_{R} being the right-handed projection operator.

Each operator carries a Wilson coefficient CiC_{i}. Since the operators are already dimension 6, Ci≡1/Λ2C_{i}\equiv 1/\Lambda^{2} carry two units of inverse mass dimension, [mass]-2. Given new physics scenario, a heavy mediator can be integrated away to match the effective interaction. Equivalently, the effective scale Λ\Lambda can be identified with the heavy mediator mass up to some dimensionless coupling constants. Although there is no fundamental principle to forbidden the above operators to simultaneously appear, we consider them separately in the following discussions.

II.1 Fermionic DM Absorption on Electron and Atomic Effects

The local DM distribution around the Sun is roughly known from the hydrodynamic simulation of our Milky Way galaxy [17]. With the DM energy density, ρχ≈0.4\rho_{\chi}\approx 0.4 GeV/cm3, its number density nχ=ρχ/mχn_{\chi}=\rho_{\chi}/m_{\chi} is inversely proportional to mass mχm_{\chi}. In addition, the DM velocity distribution is determined by the gravitational potential of the galaxy matter and dark matter. Around the Sun, the DM velocity follows the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution and peaks around typically vχ∼(200∼300)v_{\chi}\sim(200\sim 300) km/s. In other words, the DM in our solar system is non-relativistic with only 𝒪⁡(10−3)\mathcal{O}(10^{-3}) of the speed of light. Since the absorption process releases the whole DM mass as the energy of final-state particles, its kinetic energy Tχ≈12​mχ​vχ2T_{\chi}\approx\frac{1}{2}m_{\chi}v^{2}_{\chi} is negligibly small, Tχ/mχ∼𝒪⁡(10−6)T_{\chi}/m_{\chi}\sim\mathcal{O}(10^{-6}). We can take both the initial electron and DM particle as at rest to estimate the scattering cross section σχ​e\sigma_{\chi e},

σχ​eS​vχ\displaystyle\sigma^{S}_{\chi e}v_{\chi} ≈\displaystyle\approx 1Λ4​mχ2​(2​me+mχ)464​π​(me+mχ)4,\displaystyle\frac{1}{\Lambda^{4}}\frac{m_{\chi}^{2}(2m_{e}+m_{\chi})^{4}}{64\pi(m_{e}+m_{\chi})^{4}}, (2a)
σχ​eP​vχ\displaystyle\sigma^{P}_{\chi e}v_{\chi} ≈\displaystyle\approx 1Λ4​mχ4​(2​me+mχ)264​π​(me+mχ)4,\displaystyle\frac{1}{\Lambda^{4}}\frac{m_{\chi}^{4}(2m_{e}+m_{\chi})^{2}}{64\pi(m_{e}+m_{\chi})^{4}}, (2b)
σχ​eV​vχ\displaystyle\sigma^{V}_{\chi e}v_{\chi} ≈\displaystyle\approx 1Λ4​mχ2​(2​me+mχ)2​(2​me2+4​me​mχ+3​mχ2)32​π​(me+mχ)4,\displaystyle\frac{1}{\Lambda^{4}}{m_{\chi}^{2}(2m_{e}+m_{\chi})^{2}(2m_{e}^{2}+4m_{e}m_{\chi}+3m_{\chi}^{2})\over 32\pi(m_{e}+m_{\chi})^{4}}, (2c)
σχ​eA​vχ\displaystyle\sigma^{A}_{\chi e}v_{\chi} ≈\displaystyle\approx 1Λ4​mχ2​(2​me+mχ)2​(6​me2+8​me​mχ+3​mχ2)32​π​(me+mχ)4,\displaystyle\frac{1}{\Lambda^{4}}{m_{\chi}^{2}(2m_{e}+m_{\chi})^{2}(6m_{e}^{2}+8m_{e}m_{\chi}+3m_{\chi}^{2})\over 32\pi(m_{e}+m_{\chi})^{4}}, (2d)
σχ​eT​vχ\displaystyle\sigma^{T}_{\chi e}v_{\chi} ≈\displaystyle\approx 1Λ4​mχ2​(2​me+mχ)2​(6​me2+10​me​mχ+5​mχ2)8​π​(me+mχ)4.\displaystyle\frac{1}{\Lambda^{4}}{m_{\chi}^{2}(2m_{e}+m_{\chi})^{2}(6m_{e}^{2}+10m_{e}m_{\chi}+5m_{\chi}^{2})\over 8\pi(m_{e}+m_{\chi})^{4}}. (2e)

Those terms suppressed by the DM velocity vχv_{\chi} have been neglected for clarity. Nevertheless, the DM velocity does not disappear completely since the quantity that enters the DM event rate is σχ​e​vχ\sigma_{\chi e}v_{\chi} as a whole. In the limit of tiny DM mass, mχ≪mem_{\chi}\ll m_{e}, all cross sections reduce to a universal value, mχ2/4​π​Λ4m^{2}_{\chi}/4\pi\Lambda^{4} [105].

In reality, the initial and final electrons are subject to the Coulomb potential produced by the central nuclei and other surrounding electrons. There is no way for the initial electron that is confined inside the atom to be at rest. Not to say for a typical 𝒪⁡(CLOSE\mathcal{O}(keV) electron recoil, its kinetic energy is of the same size as the binding energy. The atomic binding effect could be large enough to affect the direct detection event rate. We follow the general formalism developed with second quantization for both the initial bound and final ionized electron states [111]. The differential cross section is then a convolution of the particle scattering amplitude |ℳ|2|\mathcal{M}|^{2} and the atomic KK-factor Kn​l​(Tr,|𝐪|)K_{nl}(T_{r},|{\bf q}|),

d​σχ​ed​Tr​vχ=1Tr​∑n​l(4​l+2)​∫d3​𝐪(2​π)3​2​Eν​18​me2​Eχ​|ℳ|2​(𝐪)​Kn​l​(Tr,|𝐪|)​(2​π)​δE,\displaystyle\frac{d\sigma_{\chi e}}{dT_{r}}v_{\chi}=\frac{1}{T_{r}}\sum_{nl}(4l+2)\int\frac{d^{3}{\bf q}}{(2\pi)^{3}2E_{\nu}}\frac{1}{8m_{e}^{2}E_{\chi}}|\mathcal{M}|^{2}({\bf q})K_{nl}(T_{r},|{\bf q}|)(2\pi)\delta_{E}, (3)

The summation over the principle quantum number nn and the angular momentum ll is a product of the electron number (2​l+1)(2l+1) of the state |n​l⟩\ket{nl} and the spin degree of freedom 22.

The remaining δE\delta_{E} function comes from energy conservation. For non-relativistic DM, its kinetic energy can be omitted in comparsion with the energy release from the DM absorption process,

δE≡δ⁡(mχ−|𝐪|−Δ​En​l).\displaystyle\delta_{E}\equiv\delta(m_{\chi}-|{\bf q}|-\Delta E_{nl}). (4)

With vanishing mass, the neutrino energy Eν=|𝐪|E_{\nu}=|{\bf q}| is the same as its momentum and equivalently the size of momentum transfer |𝐪||{\bf q}|. On the electron side, the energy gain, Δ​En​l≡Tr−En​l\Delta E_{nl}\equiv T_{r}-E_{nl}, is the difference between the ionized electron energy TrT_{r} and the negative initial binding energy En​lE_{nl} for the state |n​l⟩|nl\rangle. It is then desirable to first integrate |𝐪||{\bf q}| away from the phase space element d3​𝐪=|𝐪|2​d​|𝐪|​d​Ωqd^{3}{\bf q}=|{\bf q}|^{2}d|{\bf q}|d\Omega_{q}. For the scattering with a bound electron, |𝐪||{\bf q}| and TrT_{r} are usually independent variables due to the unknown initial electron momentum inside an atom. However, the energy conservation (4) establishes a correlation, |𝐪|=mχ−Δ​En​l|{\bf q}|=m_{\chi}-\Delta E_{nl}.

On the other hand, the solid angle integration dΩq≡dcosθqdϕqd\Omega_{q}\equiv d\cos\theta_{q}d\phi_{q} contains the information of momentum transfer direction. However, neither the KK-factor Kn​l​(Tr,|𝐪|)K_{nl}(T_{r},|{\bf q}|) [111] nor the scattering matrix element |ℳ⁡(𝐪)|2|\mathcal{M}({\bf q})|^{2} has dependence on the angular coordinates of 𝐪{\bf q}. For the latter, the angular independence happens due to the fact that the DM velocity is negligible in the absorption process. Without a preference, the direction of 𝐪{\bf q} is not important either. The solid angle integration then simply gives an overall 4​π4\pi. Consequently, (3) becomes,

d⁡⟨σχ​e​vχ⟩d​Tr=∑n​l(4​l+2)​1Tr​mχ−Δ​En​l16​π​me2​mχ​|ℳ|2​(𝐪)​Kn​l​(Tr,|𝐪|),\displaystyle\frac{d\langle\sigma_{\chi e}v_{\chi}\rangle}{dT_{r}}=\sum_{nl}(4l+2)\frac{1}{T_{r}}\frac{m_{\chi}-\Delta E_{nl}}{16\pi m^{2}_{e}m_{\chi}}|\mathcal{M}|^{2}({\bf q})K_{nl}(T_{r},|{\bf q}|), (5)

where we have implemented the facts that Eν=|𝐪|E_{\nu}=|{\bf q}| and |𝐪|=mχ−Δ​En​l|{\bf q}|=m_{\chi}-\Delta E_{nl}. Since the left-hand sides of (3) and (5) are independent of the DM velocity, σχ​e​vχ\sigma_{\chi e}v_{\chi} is essentially ⟨σχ​e​vχ⟩\langle\sigma_{\chi e}v_{\chi}\rangle. Although there are five operators in (1), the scattering matrix element |ℳ|2|\mathcal{M}|^{2} has only two different forms,

|ℳ(S,V,A,T)|2=(4,4,12,48)×1Λ4​mχ​me2​(mχ−Δ​En​l),|ℳP|2=1Λ4​mχ​(mχ−Δ​En​l)3.\displaystyle\left|\mathcal{M}^{(S,V,A,T)}\right|^{2}=(4,4,12,48)\times\frac{1}{\Lambda^{4}}m_{\chi}m^{2}_{e}(m_{\chi}-\Delta E_{nl}),\qquad\left|\mathcal{M}^{P}\right|^{2}=\frac{1}{\Lambda^{4}}m_{\chi}(m_{\chi}-\Delta E_{nl})^{3}. (6)

The pseudo-scalar (P) case is quite special since the matrix element intrinsically has momentum transfer dependence as elaborated in [111]. For comparison, the others have exactly the same structure.

The left panel of Fig. 1 shows the typical differential and total cross sections for mχ=(59,105)m_{\chi}=(59,105) keV. Since the scalar, vector, axial vector, and tensor interactions share the same matrix element structure and consequently the same differential spectrum, only vector (blue) and pseudo-scalar (green) curves are shown. For comparison, the electron recoil energy from the DM absorption on a free electron at rest takes a fixed value (gray), Tr=mχ2/2​(me+mχ)T_{r}=m^{2}_{\chi}/2(m_{e}+m_{\chi}) which is derived without approximation. Although the spectrum widens due to atomic effect, the peak is still at exactly the same location as the free case. For mχ=(59,105)m_{\chi}=(59,105) keV, the peak position is Tr=(3.05,8.95)T_{r}=(3.05,8.95) keV, respectively. We have adjusted the yy-axis scales for the vector (left blue) and pseudo-scalar (right green) cases to make the mχ=105m_{\chi}=105 keV peaks with roughly the same height. Since the matrix element |ℳ|2|\mathcal{M}|^{2} has mχ−Δ​En​lm_{\chi}-\Delta E_{nl} dependence for the vector operator and (mχ−Δ​En​l)3(m_{\chi}-\Delta E_{nl})^{3} for the pseudo-scalar one, the mχ=59m_{\chi}=59 keV peak heights scale accordingly. With major contribution coming from the outer shell electrons, the binding energy Eb=(0.16,0.012)E_{b}=(0.16,0.012) keV for (4​p4p, 5​p5p) shells can be negligibly small. Then the peak height scales with mχ−Trm_{\chi}-T_{r} and (mχ−Tr)3(m_{\chi}-T_{r})^{3}, respectively. For the vector (pseudo-scalar) case, the peak height reduces by a factor of 0.58 (0.20). This explains why the pseudo-scalar peak is only around 1/31/3 of the vector counterpart for mχ=59m_{\chi}=59 keV. The TrT_{r} dependence arises from the KK-factor and energy gain Δ​En​l=Tr−En​l\Delta E_{nl}=T_{r}-E_{nl}. Although the mχ−Trm_{\chi}-T_{r} dependence is quite different, the spectrum shape has only slight difference among operators. This is because the two cases shown in the left panel of Fig. 1 has mχ≫Trm_{\chi}\gg T_{r}. Consequently, the TrT_{r} spectrum is mainly determined by the KK-factor which is universally shared. This allows a unique probe that is model-independent, or at least operator-independent, to some extent. Once detected, fermionic DM absorption even allows in-situ measurement of the atomic KK-factor.

The right panel of Fig. 1 shows the total cross section ⟨σ​vχ⟩\langle\sigma v_{\chi}\rangle as a function of the DM mass. With larger mχm_{\chi}, the cross section also becomes larger. For light DM, mχ≪mem_{\chi}\ll m_{e}, (2) indicates that σχ​eP​vχ\sigma^{P}_{\chi e}v_{\chi} for pseudo-scalar type scales as mχ4m^{4}_{\chi} while the others as mχ2m^{2}_{\chi}. The curves for free electron scattering are fully consistent with the expected scaling behaviors. Including atomic effects would reduce the total cross section due to binding energy of the initial electron. For inner shells, such as Eb=(4.53,0.95)E_{b}=(4.53,0.95) keV for (2​p2p, 3​p3p) electrons, the binding energy can be as large as the recoil energy TrT_{r} to significantly reduce the event rate. The green lines show the ratio between the total cross sections with bound and free electrons. A reduction of 0.5∼0.70.5\sim 0.7 can happen. With smaller mχm_{\chi}, the energy release is also smaller and consequently harder to overcome the atomic bound energy which leads to a larger suppression in the total cross section.

II.2 Confronting the Xenon1T and PandaX-II Data

In 2020, both Xenon1T and PandaX-II collaborations published their electron recoil spectrum [106, 112]. An excess around (2∼3)(2\sim 3) keV appears in the Xenon1T data with significance reaching 3​σ3\sigma. This could be explained by the β\beta decays of tritium at 3.2​σ3.2\sigma with a concentration in xenon of (6.2±2.0)×10−25(6.2\pm 2.0)\times 10^{-25} mol/mol, but “such a trace amount can neither be confirmed nor excluded ” [106]. The PandaX-II data is fully consistent with such a founding [112]. Since a sub-MeV fermionic DM absorption also leaves a sharp peak at low recoil energy as shown in Fig. 1, confronting the the Xenon1T and PandaX-II data can also provide a meaningful constraint on the preferred parameter space.

The event rate of DM direct detection,

d​Nd​Tr=NT​ρχmχ​t×ϵ⁡(Tr)​d⁡⟨σχ​e​vχ⟩d​Tr,\displaystyle\frac{dN}{dT_{r}}=N_{T}\frac{\rho_{\chi}}{m_{\chi}}t\times\epsilon(T_{r})\frac{d\langle\sigma_{\chi e}v_{\chi}\rangle}{dT_{r}}, (7)

scales with for the number of Xenon atoms NTN_{T}, DM local number density ρχ/mχ\rho_{\chi}/m_{\chi}, and run time tt. The Xenon1T analysis uses 0.65 tonne-years of data and PandaX-II 100 has tonne-days. In addition, the detection efficiencies are basically constant above (3∼4)(3\sim 4) keV and decreases to 0 below there [106].

We adopt the analytical χ2\chi^{2} analysis [113, 114], whose advanced version is summarized in App. A, to estimate the sensitivity. In addition to the fermionic DM absorption signal, background estimations are taken from the experimental papers [106]. The results are shown in Fig. 2 for the fit with Xenon1T (left panel) and PandaX-II (right panel) data. Since the different DM absorption operators share roughly the same spectrum shape, one representative vector case can already show the features clearly. For Xenon1T, the best fit is at mχ=59m_{\chi}=59 keV and Λ=1\Lambda=1 TeV, being consistent with [105]. The inset plot shows the signal and background curves with the best fit values. The fermionic DM absorption signal with peak at Tr=3.1T_{r}=3.1 keV can fit the Xenon1T excess very nicely. Comparing with the background-only fit, the χmin2\chi^{2}_{\rm min} decreases from 46.3 to 32.2. The decreasing edge for mχ→20m_{\chi}\rightarrow 20 keV is due to two major reasons: 1) the cross section decreases with mχ2m^{2}_{\chi} in this region and 2) the efficiency further suppresses its event rate to make it less sensitive. Both needs compensation of a larger coupling strength, or equivalently a lower cut-off scale Λ\Lambda. On the other side, the rising edge for mχ→150m_{\chi}\rightarrow 150 keV at Xenon1T is due to the abormally lower data point around (17∼18)(17\sim 18) keV where the recoil spectrum peaks. For PandaX-II data [112], the best fit is at mχ=105m_{\chi}=105 keV corresponding to the small excess at Tr=(8∼9)T_{r}=(8\sim 9) keV. Since the peak is not that significant, the χmin2\chi^{2}_{\rm min} decreases by only less than 3 from 31.0 of the background-only fit to 28.3. Different from the Xenon1T data, the Tr=(17∼19)T_{r}=(17\sim 19) keV data points are higher than the expected background instead which leads to a flat tail for mχ→150m_{\chi}\rightarrow 150 keV.

III The DM overproduction in the early universe

A light DM is typically produced non-thermally. This is because the thermal freeze-out give a relic density ρχ∝mχ2/⟨σ​v⟩\rho_{\chi}\propto m^{2}_{\chi}/\langle\sigma v\rangle as ratio between the DM mass and the thermally averaged cross section [115]. To obtain the correct relic density, the interaction strength between DM and SM particles should scale linearly with its mass. Consequently, a light DM typically has a very small coupling with SM particles. Then it is difficult for the light DM to reach thermal equilibrium with the environmental plasma before the thermal freeze-out [116]. Their production is usually realized by the so-called freeze-in mechanism [117, 119, 118, 120, 121]. No matter how the DM relic density is generated, it cannot exceed the observed value, Ωdm​h2≈0.12\Omega_{\rm dm}h^{2}\approx 0.12 [122].

III.1 Boltzmann Equation and Its Solution

For the fermionic DM absorption on electron target, it is intrinsically connected to electron and positron as demonstrated by the operators in (1). The light DM can be produced by the pair annihilation process e+​e−→χ​νe^{+}e^{-}\to\chi\nu. The Boltzmann equation governing the evolution of DM number density nχn_{\chi} is,

d​nχd​t+3​H​nχ\displaystyle{dn_{\chi}\over dt}+3Hn_{\chi} =\displaystyle= ∫d​Πχ​d​Πν​d​Πe−​d​Πe+​(2​π)4​δ(4)​(pe++pe−−pχ−pν)\displaystyle\int d\Pi_{\chi}d\Pi_{\nu}d\Pi_{e^{-}}d\Pi_{e^{+}}(2\pi)^{4}\delta^{(4)}(p_{e^{+}}+p_{e^{-}}-p_{\chi}-p_{\nu}) (8)
×\displaystyle\times [|ℳ|e+​e−→ν​χ2​fe+​fe−​(1−fν)​(1−fχ)−|​ℳ|ν​χ→e+​e−2​fν​fχ​(1−fe+)​(1−fe−)],\displaystyle\left[|{\cal M}|_{e^{+}e^{-}\to\nu\chi}^{2}f_{e^{+}}f_{e^{-}}(1-f_{\nu})(1-f_{\chi})-|{\cal M}|_{\nu\chi\to e^{+}e^{-}}^{2}f_{\nu}f_{\chi}(1-f_{e^{+}})(1-f_{e^{-}})\right],

where HH is the Hubble parameter. For particle ii, fif_{i} is its phase space distribution function and d​Πi≡d3​pi/2​Ei​(2​π)3d\Pi_{i}\equiv d^{3}p_{i}/2E_{i}(2\pi)^{3} is the phase space integration element.

With the freeze-in mechanism, the DM density increases from 0. During the production process, fχ≪fe+,fe−f_{\chi}\ll f_{e^{+}},f_{e^{-}}. For simplicity, the second term of (8) can be omitted [121] and the Boltzmann equation then reduces to,

d​nχd​t+3​H​nχ\displaystyle{dn_{\chi}\over dt}+3Hn_{\chi} =\displaystyle= ⟨vMøl​σe+​e−⟩​ne+eq​ne−eq,\displaystyle\langle v_{\rm M\o l}\sigma_{e^{+}e^{-}}\rangle n_{e^{+}}^{\rm eq}n_{e^{-}}^{\rm eq}, (9)

where vMølv_{\rm M\o l} is the Mø\oller velocity of incoming electron/positron pair [123] and ne±eqn^{\rm eq}_{e^{\pm}} are their number density at thermal equilibrium. We will come back to provide a detailed justification of this simplification later.

To solve the Boltzmann equation, we introduce the DM yield Y≡nχ/s⁡(T)Y\equiv n_{\chi}/s(T) as the ratio of DM number density nχn_{\chi} over the entropy density s⁡(T)s(T) as a function of temperature TT. At the epoch of DM production, the universe is dominated by radiation. Both the Hubble parameter HH and entropy density s⁡(T)s(T) can evolve with temperature,

H=1.66​g∗​T2MP,s⁡(T)=g∗s​2​π245​T3,\displaystyle H=1.66\sqrt{g_{*}}{T^{2}\over M_{\rm P}},\qquad s(T)=g_{*s}{2\pi^{2}\over 45}T^{3}, (10)

where MP=1.22×1019​GeVM_{P}=1.22\times 10^{19}~\rm GeV is the Planck mass. The relativistic degrees of freedom g∗=g∗​(T)g_{*}=g_{*}(T) and g∗s=g∗s​(T)g_{*s}=g_{*s}(T) associated with the energy and entropy densities, respectively, are taken from [124] while more detailed discussions can be found in [125, 126]. Although the DM yield keeps increasing, the effective degrees of freedom are mainly contributed by the SM particles. Then in terms of yield YY, the Boltzmann equation (9) becomes,

d​Yd​T=−45​MP2​π2​(1.66​g∗)​g~∗s​T6​⟨vMøl​σe+​e−⟩​ne+eq​ne−eq,withg~∗s≡g∗s​(1+T3​g∗s​d​g∗sd​T)−1.\displaystyle{dY\over dT}=-{45M_{\rm P}\over 2\pi^{2}(1.66\sqrt{g_{*}})\tilde{g}_{*s}T^{6}}\langle v_{\rm M\o l}\sigma_{e^{+}e^{-}}\rangle n_{e^{+}}^{\rm eq}n_{e^{-}}^{\rm eq},\quad\mbox{with}\quad\tilde{g}_{*s}\equiv g_{*s}\left(1+{T\over 3g_{*s}}{dg_{*s}\over dT}\right)^{-1}. (11)

The minus sign in d​Y/d​TdY/dT arises because the temperature decreases with time but the DM yield YY increases.

The electron and positron annihilation e+​e−→χ​νe^{+}e^{-}\rightarrow\chi\nu happens when the temperature decreases to around the electron mass, T∼2​meT\sim 2m_{e} [127]. Then the inverse process χ​ν→e+​e−\chi\nu\rightarrow e^{+}e^{-} starts to decrease and the e±e^{\pm} density becomes exponentially suppressed. In other words, the Fermi-Dirac distribution of electron (positron) can be approximated by the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution fe±eq≈e−E/Tf_{e^{\pm}}^{\rm eq}\approx e^{-E/T}. For quantitative illustration, the typical electron (positron) energy is Ee≈2.27E_{e}\approx 2.27 MeV at T≈1T\approx 1 MeV to Ee≈1.01E_{e}\approx 1.01 MeV at T≈0.4T\approx 0.4 MeV. Correspondingly, the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution gives e−E/T=0.104e^{-E/T}=0.104 at T≈1T\approx 1 MeV and 0.0800.080 at T≈0.4T\approx 0.4 MeV, which are very close to the Fermi-Dirac values 0.0940.094 and 0.0740.074, respectively. This further simplifies the thermally averaged cross section ⟨vMøl​σe+​e−⟩\langle v_{\rm M\o l}\sigma_{e^{+}e^{-}}\rangle [123],

⟨vMøl​σe+​e−⟩​ne+eq​ne−eq=T8​π4​∫4​me2∞d​s​(s−4​me2)​s​K1​(sT)​σe+​e−​(s),\displaystyle\langle v_{\rm M\o l}\sigma_{e^{+}e^{-}}\rangle n_{e^{+}}^{\rm eq}n_{e^{-}}^{\rm eq}={T\over 8\pi^{4}}\int_{4m_{e}^{2}}^{\infty}ds(s-4m_{e}^{2})\sqrt{s}K_{1}\left({\sqrt{s}\over T}\right)\sigma_{e^{+}e^{-}}(s), (12)

where K1K_{1} is the first modified Bessel function of second kind and s≡(pe−+pe+)2s\equiv(p_{e^{-}}+p_{e^{+}})^{2} is the electron positron invariant mass squared.

The solution of the Boltzmann equation in (11) can be obtained by integrating the temperature TT from neutrino decoupling Tmax≈1T_{\rm max}\approx 1 MeV,

Y⁡(T)=45​MP16​π6​∫TTmaxd​T~(1.66​g∗)​g~∗s​T~5​∫4​me2∞d​s​(s−4​me2)​s​K1​(sT~)​σe−​e+​(s).\displaystyle Y(T)={45M_{\rm P}\over 16\pi^{6}}\int_{T}^{T_{\rm max}}{d\widetilde{T}\over(1.66\sqrt{g_{*}})\tilde{g}_{*s}\widetilde{T}^{5}}\int_{4m_{e}^{2}}^{\infty}ds(s-4m_{e}^{2})\sqrt{s}K_{1}\left({\sqrt{s}\over\widetilde{T}}\right)\sigma_{e^{-}e^{+}}(s). (13)

For the DM absorption operators in (1), the e−​e+→ν​χe^{-}e^{+}\to\nu\chi cross section is a function of the invariant mass ss,
