Fig. 3 shows the evolution of the DM yield Y⁡(T)Y(T) as a function of temperature TT. For illustration, we adopt the scale Λ=1\Lambda=1 TeV and DM mass mχ=60m_{\chi}=60 keV. For all the five DM absorption operators, the DM yield converges when the Universe cools down to T∼0.4T\sim 0.4 MeV. In the light DM limit, mχ≪me≲sm_{\chi}\ll m_{e}\lesssim\sqrt{s}, the cross sections in (14) have quite simple scaling behaviors, σe+​e−S,P,V,A,T≈(18,18,16,16,13)×s/4​π​Λ4\sigma^{S,P,V,A,T}_{e^{+}e^{-}}\approx(\frac{1}{8},\frac{1}{8},\frac{1}{6},\frac{1}{6},\frac{1}{3})\times s/4\pi\Lambda^{4}. There is no big difference among scalar and pseudo-scalar operators or among the vector and axial vector ones as correctly reflected in Fig. 3. With larger cross section, the DM yield converges to a larger value. Between the scalar/pseudoscalar group and the vector/axial vector group, the converging values of the DM yield roughly differs by a factor of 3/4 which is consistent with the relative size among the cross sections, σe+​e−S,P/σe+​e−V,A≈3/4\sigma^{S,P}_{e^{+}e^{-}}/\sigma^{V,A}_{e^{+}e^{-}}\approx 3/4. The small deivation comes from the finite size of the DM mass mχ=60m_{\chi}=60 keV that is used in Fig. 14. The DM yield scales linearly with the e+​e−→χ​νe^{+}e^{-}\rightarrow\chi\nu cross section. We can also check that between the vector/axial vector group and the tensor operator, the factor of 2 difference is also consistent with both sides.

III.2 Consistency Check of the Simplified Boltzmann Equation

Before proceeding to constrain the coupling strength of the DM absorption operators, we need to first justify the omission of the second term in (8) for consistency check. The freeze-in production of DM spans from neutrino decoupling (T∼1T\sim 1 MeV) to the end of e+​e−e^{+}e^{-} annihilation (T∼0.1T\sim 0.1 MeV) [127]. During this period of time, electrons and positrons are still in equilibrium with the thermal bath and therefore follow the Fermi-Dirac distribution, fe±≡1/(eEe±/T+1)f_{e^{\pm}}\equiv{1/(e^{E_{e^{\pm}}/T}+1)}. The most likely value of the electron/positron energy maximizes the energy distribution Ee2−me2​Ee​feeq\sqrt{E_{e}^{2}-m_{e}^{2}}E_{e}f_{e}^{\rm eq}. For example, the peak energy is Ee≈2.27E_{e}\approx 2.27 MeV at T≈1T\approx 1 MeV and Ee≈1.01E_{e}\approx 1.01 MeV at T≈0.4T\approx 0.4 MeV. Correspondingly, the phase space distribution function is roughly feeq∼0.094f_{e}^{\rm eq}\sim 0.094 (0.074) at T≈1​MeVT\approx 1\,\rm MeV (0.4​MeV0.4\,\rm MeV). Therefore, we can approximate (1−fe±)≈1(1-f_{e^{\pm}})\approx 1 in the second term of (8).

The cosmological evolution of DM density is related to the observed number density nχ0=ρχ/mχn^{0}_{\chi}=\rho_{\chi}/m_{\chi} today. Especially, the maximal value of nχn_{\chi} at the end of freeze-in process is nχ0/a3n^{0}_{\chi}/a^{3} neglecting the possible DM decay. At temperature T=0.4T=0.4 MeV, the scale factor a≡1/(1+z)a\equiv 1/(1+z) or equivalently the redshift is z≈1/a≈1.6×109z\approx 1/a\approx 1.6\times 10^{9} [1]. The upper limit is reached when the freeze-in process contributes the full DM density. Since the DM is not in thermal equilibrium, one can only use the typical energy E¯χ\overline{E}_{\chi} to estimate the size of the phase space distribution function,

nχ=∫d3​p(2​π)3​fχ≈12​π2​fχ​(E¯χ)​E¯χ3≲nχ0a3≈ρχ0mχ​z3≈4×10−5​MeV3​keVmχ.\displaystyle n_{\chi}=\int{d^{3}p\over(2\pi)^{3}}f_{\chi}\approx{1\over 2\pi^{2}}f_{\chi}(\overline{E}_{\chi})\overline{E}_{\chi}^{3}\lesssim{n^{0}_{\chi}\over a^{3}}\approx{\rho^{0}_{\chi}\over m_{\chi}}z^{3}\approx 4\times 10^{-5}~{\rm MeV^{3}}{{\rm keV}\over m_{\chi}}. (15)

The typical DM energy can be determined using the energy conservation condition Eχ+Eν=Ee++Ee−E_{\chi}+E_{\nu}=E_{e^{+}}+E_{e^{-}} with the typical electron and positron energies Ee±E_{e^{\pm}}. In a head-on collision and Ee+=Ee−E_{e+}=E_{e^{-}}, the neutrino energy Eν=Eχ2−mχ2E_{\nu}=\sqrt{E_{\chi}^{2}-m_{\chi}^{2}} is directly related to the DM momentum and the DM energy is solved to be Eχ=[mχ2+(Ee−+Ee+)2]/[2​(Ee−+Ee+)]E_{\chi}=[m_{\chi}^{2}+(E_{e^{-}}+E_{e^{+}})^{2}]/[2(E_{e^{-}}+E_{e^{+}})]. For a sub-MeV DM with mχ≪Ee±m_{\chi}\ll E_{e^{\pm}}, the DM energy has a lower limit, Eχ≳(Ee−+Ee+)/2E_{\chi}\gtrsim(E_{e^{-}}+E_{e^{+}})/2 which is approximately 1 MeV at T≈0.4​MeVT\approx 0.4\,\rm MeV. The typical DM phase space factor is then bounded from above,

fχ≲4×10−5​MeV3​keVmχ​2​π2E¯χ3≈8×10−4​keVmχ,\displaystyle f_{\chi}\lesssim 4\times 10^{-5}~{\rm MeV^{3}}{{\rm keV}\over m_{\chi}}{2\pi^{2}\over\overline{E}_{\chi}^{3}}\approx 8\times 10^{-4}{{\rm keV}\over m_{\chi}}, (16)

which is truly small comparing the electron counterpat, fe∼0.1f_{e}\sim 0.1.

For the neutrino phase space distribution fνf_{\nu}, there are two components. One is the standard cosmic neutrino background that was in thermal equilibrium and follows the Fermi-Dirac distribution fνeq≡1/(eEν/T+1)f_{\nu}^{\rm eq}\equiv 1/(e^{E_{\nu}/T}+1). The other one is the associated production from e+​e−→χ​νe^{+}e^{-}\rightarrow\chi\nu that shares a similar contribution (fν≲10−3f_{\nu}\lesssim 10^{-3}) as DM. So we can approximate fν≈fνeqf_{\nu}\approx f_{\nu}^{\rm eq}. Based on a similar analysis as for feeqf_{e}^{\rm eq} by requiring that Eν2​fνeqE_{\nu}^{2}f_{\nu}^{\rm eq} takes its maximal value, one can obtain the typical neutrino energy Eν≈2.22​(0.89)​MeVE_{\nu}\approx 2.22\,(0.89)\,\rm MeV at T≈1​(0.4)​MeVT\approx 1\,(0.4)\,\rm MeV. This further leads to a typical phase space distribution fνeq≈0.1f_{\nu}^{\rm eq}\approx 0.1. With massless neutrino, this estimation is independent of TT since its phase space distribution function only depends on the ratio Eν/TE_{\nu}/T. Therefore, we also approximate 1−fν≈11-f_{\nu}\approx 1 to very good accuracy.

Putting things (fe±f_{e^{\pm}}, fχf_{\chi}, and fνf_{\nu}) together, we can justify the simplification of omitting the second term in (8). At the converging point (T≈0.4​MeVT\approx 0.4\,\rm MeV) of DM yield, the phase space factor ratio

fe+​fe−fν​f¯χ≳61​mχkeV≫1,\displaystyle{f_{e^{+}}f_{e^{-}}\over f_{\nu}\bar{f}_{\chi}}\gtrsim 61{m_{\chi}\over{\rm keV}}\gg 1, (17)

for the sub-MeV DM 1​keV≲mχ≲1​MeV1\,{\rm keV}\lesssim m_{\chi}\lesssim 1\,{\rm MeV} clearly indicates that the first term of (8) dominates over the second one [121].

III.3 Constraints from DM Overproduction

To estimate the DM yield today Y0Y_{0}, we assume there is no other mechanisms to produce/deplete DM after its production after the converging point TminT_{\rm min}. Then Y0=Y⁡(Tmin)Y_{0}=Y(T_{\rm min}) with time-independence since both the DM number density nχn_{\chi} and the entropy density ss scales as 1/a31/a^{3}. The DM relic density is estimated as,

Ωχ​h2=2​mχ​Y0​s0​h2ρc,\displaystyle\Omega_{\chi}h^{2}={2m_{\chi}Y_{0}s_{0}h^{2}\over\rho_{c}}, (18)

where s0=2970​cm−3s_{0}=2970\,\rm cm^{-3} is the present entropy density and ρc=1.054×10−5​h2​GeV​cm−3\rho_{c}=1.054\times 10^{-5}h^{2}\,\rm GeV\,cm^{-3} the critical density. The Hubble constant h=0.67h=0.67 is in unit of 100​km​s−1​Mpc−1100\,\rm km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}. Since both DM and its anti-particle can be produced, there is a factor of 2 in the above estimation. Requiring the DM relic density to be less than the measured value, Ωχ​h2≲0.12\Omega_{\chi}h^{2}\lesssim 0.12, sets a lower bound on the new physics scale Λ\Lambda of the DM absorption operators in (1). In other words, the DM relic density cannot be overproduced.

Fig. 4 shows the constraints on the direct detection cross section σχ​e​vχ\sigma_{\chi e}v_{\chi}. The excluded parameter space by the DM overproduction is shown as filled region with dashed boundary. These DM overproduction bounds are quite stringent in the low mass region, especially for the pseudo-scalar case. This is because for mχ≪2​mem_{\chi}\ll 2m_{e}, the cross-section scales as σe−​e+∝1/Λ4\sigma_{e^{-}e^{+}}\propto 1/\Lambda^{4} and becomes independent of the DM mass according to (14). Consequently, the DM yield YY estimated by (13) is not sensitive to mχm_{\chi} and the DM relic density scales as Ωχ​h2∝mχ/Λ4\Omega_{\chi}h^{2}\propto m_{\chi}/\Lambda^{4}. However, the direct detection cross section in (2) scales as power of the DM mass, σχ​eP​vχ∝mχ4/Λ4∝mχ3​Ωχ\sigma_{\chi e}^{P}v_{\chi}\propto m^{4}_{\chi}/\Lambda^{4}\propto m_{\chi}^{3}\Omega_{\chi} for the pseudo-scalar case and σχ​eV,S,A,T​vχ∝mχ2/Λ4∝mχ​Ωχ\sigma_{\chi e}^{V,S,A,T}v_{\chi}\propto m_{\chi}^{2}/\Lambda^{4}\propto m_{\chi}\Omega_{\chi} for the others. This explains why the pseudo-scalar bound decreases faster with mχm_{\chi}. For the scalar, (axial-)vector, and tensor cases, they have a similar sensitivity around 10−50​cm210^{-50}\,\rm cm^{2} to 10−47​cm210^{-47}\,\rm cm^{2} for the DM mass from 1 keV to 1 MeV.

Using the more exactly calculated cross section σχ​e​vχ\sigma_{\chi e}v_{\chi} as summarized in (2), instead of the approximation mχ2/4​π​Λ4m^{2}_{\chi}/4\pi\Lambda^{4} in the mχ≪mem_{\chi}\ll m_{e} limit, for the vertical axis has some advantage. As explained below (14), the e+​e−→χ​νe^{+}e^{-}\rightarrow\chi\nu cross section almost degenerates between scalar (σe+​e−S\sigma^{S}_{e^{+}e^{-}}) and pseudo-scalar (σe+​e−P\sigma^{P}_{e^{+}e^{-}}) operators. So one may expect their overproduction limits not to differ much and hard to distinguish in Fig. 4 is the universal mχ2/4​π​Λ4m^{2}_{\chi}/4\pi\Lambda^{4} is adopted. In contrast, the direct detection cross sections σχ​eS​vχ\sigma^{S}_{\chi e}v_{\chi} and σχ​eP​vχ\sigma^{P}_{\chi e}v_{\chi} have quite different scaling behaviors as discussed around (2). So we can still see the clear difference between the scalar and pseudo-scalar cases in Fig. 4. In addition, σχ​e\sigma_{\chi e} also has the advantage of being able to reflect the realistic direct detection signal strength.

For comparison, the best fit points (star) with the Xenon1T (light green) and PandaX-II (yellow) are also shown. The best fit values are taken from Fig. 2 for the vector case. We can see that for both data sets, the best fit points are already at the boundary of the DM overproduction constraints. Also shown are the 95% C.L. allowed regions for the Xenon1T (light green contour) and PandaX-II (yellow contour) data. Consistent with the 95% C.L. contours in Fig. 2, the 95% C.L. allowed parameter space here is divided into 2 (3) regions for the Xenon1T (PandaX-II) data. The regions extend significantly down to a few keV of the DM mass mχm_{\chi}. More discussions about the cosmological constraint from the Universe expansion history and the astrophysical ones from various X(gamma)-ray observations will be discussed later in Sec. V.1 and Sec. V.2, respectively.

IV DM decay

One important feature of the DM absorption process is that only one DM particle can appear in the process as demonstrated by the general fermionic DM absorption operators in (1). A natural consequence is that DM is unstable and can decay into light SM particles unless forbidden by kinematics. Since the DM particle is neutral, electron and positron should appear as a pair if such decay topology is possible. For χ→e+​e−+⋯\chi\rightarrow e^{+}e^{-}+\cdots to happen, the DM mass has to be larger that twice of the electron mass, mχ>2​mem_{\chi}>2m_{e}, which is already outside the mass range considered in the current paper. The only possible decay products are the neutrinos and photons.

With the DM particle being a fermion, the final state has to contain an odd number of neutrinos, including the visible decay modes (χ→ν+γ\chi\to\nu+\gamma, χ→ν+γ​γ\chi\to\nu+\gamma\gamma, and χ→ν+γ​γ​γ\chi\to\nu+\gamma\gamma\gamma) as well as the invisible mode χ→3​ν\chi\to 3\nu. All these can happen only at loop level since the absorption operators in (1) contains two electron fields. The leading 1-loop Feynman diagrams are listed in Fig. 5. For the visible decay modes, only electromagnetic interaction of the SM is needed in addition to the absorption operator. In contrast, the invisible decay mode χ→3​ν\chi\to 3\nu requires the SM weak interactions with W/ZW/Z mediator.

To have a better understanding of the connection between operators and decay processes, Tab. 1 summarizes the leading decay channels for each operator highlighted with a checkmark (✓\checkmark). The cross (×\times) indicates the decay channel that cannot be generated at 1-loop level. Although some can appear at two-loop level, they are hugely suppressed by loop factor, the weak scale, and/or phase space. For the χ→ν​γ​γ​γ\chi\to\nu\gamma\gamma\gamma and χ→3​ν\chi\to 3\nu channels from the tensor operator, the ×!\times! symbol is used to indicate that such processes can be generated at 1-loop order but heavily suppressed. In the following subsections we detail our calculation for each operator. The calculated decay width and spectrum are further used in Sec. V to derive the cosmological and astrophysical constraints.

IV.0.1 The Scalar and Pseudoscalar Operators 𝒪e​ν​χS⁡(P){\cal O}_{e\nu\chi}^{S(P)}

For the operators 𝒪e​ν​χS,P{\cal O}_{e\nu\chi}^{S,P} with an electron scalar or pseudo-scalar current, the dominant decay mode is χ→ν+γ​γ\chi\to\nu+\gamma\gamma. Aa shown in Fig. 5(b), this process is generated through electron loop with two photons attached to the electron loop. The amplitudes from loop calculation are free from the UV divergence. Consequently, the decay widths can be calculated exactly,

Γχ→ν​γ​γS\displaystyle\Gamma_{\chi\to\nu\gamma\gamma}^{S} =\displaystyle= 1Λ4​α22048​π5​me2​mχ3​∫0mχ2d​s12​s122​(mχ2−s12)2​|FS​(η)|2,\displaystyle{1\over\Lambda^{4}}{\alpha^{2}\over 2048\pi^{5}m_{e}^{2}m_{\chi}^{3}}\int_{0}^{m_{\chi}^{2}}ds_{12}s_{12}^{2}(m_{\chi}^{2}-s_{12})^{2}|F_{S}(\eta)|^{2}, (19a)
Γχ→ν​γ​γP\displaystyle\Gamma_{\chi\to\nu\gamma\gamma}^{P} =\displaystyle= 1Λ4​α22048​π5​me2​mχ3​∫0mχ2d​s12​s122​(mχ2−s12)2​|FP​(η)|2,\displaystyle{1\over\Lambda^{4}}{\alpha^{2}\over 2048\pi^{5}m_{e}^{2}m_{\chi}^{3}}\int_{0}^{m_{\chi}^{2}}ds_{12}s_{12}^{2}(m_{\chi}^{2}-s_{12})^{2}|F_{P}(\eta)|^{2}, (19b)

where α≡e4/4​π\alpha\equiv e^{4}/4\pi is the electromagnetic fine structure constant. The integration variable s12s_{12} is the squared invariant mass of the two final-state photons, staring from 0 to the maximal value mχ2m^{2}_{\chi}. The loop functions FS,P​(η)F_{S,P}(\eta) with η≡s12/me2\eta\equiv s_{12}/m_{e}^{2} are,

FS​(η)\displaystyle F_{S}(\eta) ≡\displaystyle\equiv 4η−η−4η2​ln2​η−4−ηη−4+η,\displaystyle{4\over\eta}-{\eta-4\over\eta^{2}}\ln^{2}{\sqrt{\eta-4}-\sqrt{\eta}\over\sqrt{\eta-4}+\sqrt{\eta}}, (20a)
FP​(η)\displaystyle F_{P}(\eta) ≡\displaystyle\equiv −1η​ln2​η−4−ηη−4+η.\displaystyle-{1\over\eta}\ln^{2}{\sqrt{\eta-4}-\sqrt{\eta}\over\sqrt{\eta-4}+\sqrt{\eta}}. (20b)

In the limit of mχ≪2​mem_{\chi}\ll 2m_{e} and consequently s12≪me2s_{12}\ll m^{2}_{e}, the loop functions reduce to FS​(η)≈2/3F_{S}(\eta)\approx 2/3 and FP​(η)≈1F_{P}(\eta)\approx 1. Then the decay widths above can be approximated as,

Γχ→ν​γ​γS\displaystyle\Gamma_{\chi\to\nu\gamma\gamma}^{S} ≈\displaystyle\approx 9.4×10−20​sec−1​(mχ200​keV)7​(TeVΛ)4,\displaystyle 9.4\times 10^{-20}{\rm sec^{-1}}\left(m_{\chi}\over 200\,\rm keV\right)^{7}\left(\rm TeV\over\Lambda\right)^{4}, (21a)
Γχ→ν​γ​γP\displaystyle\Gamma_{\chi\to\nu\gamma\gamma}^{P} ≈\displaystyle\approx 2.1×10−19​sec−1​(mχ200​keV)7​(TeVΛ)4.\displaystyle 2.1\times 10^{-19}{\rm sec^{-1}}\left(m_{\chi}\over 200\,\rm keV\right)^{7}\left(\rm TeV\over\Lambda\right)^{4}. (21b)

For the 2-body mode χ→ν​γ\chi\to\nu\gamma in Fig. 5(a) and the 4-body one χ→ν​γ​γ​γ\chi\to\nu\gamma\gamma\gamma in Fig. 5(c), the electron loop contribution vanishes due to the QED (quantum electrodynamics) charge conjugation symmetry. This is because the involved electron currents e¯​e\bar{e}e and e¯​γ5​e\bar{e}\gamma_{5}e have an even parity under charge conjugation transformation while the photon field is odd. With an odd number of photons, the one-loop diagram is odd and should vanish. Non-vanishing contribution can only be generated at the 2-loop level involving both QED and weak interactions. However, such a contribution is severely suppressed by the loop factor and weak scale such as me2/mW2m_{e}^{2}/m_{W}^{2}. Therefore, we can neglect the single- and triple-photon contributions.

The 3-body invisible decay χ→3​ν\chi\to 3\nu in the last two diagrams of Fig. 5 is also vanishing. The connection between the χ​ν\chi\nu fermion lines at the top and the other two neutrinos is established through the 𝒪e​ν​χS\mathcal{O}^{S}_{e\nu\chi} and 𝒪e​ν​χP\mathcal{O}^{P}_{e\nu\chi} operators. Correspondingly, the effective current for the other two neutrinos after loop integration should also be of the same scalar feature as the e¯​e\bar{e}e and e¯​γ5​e\bar{e}\gamma_{5}e counterpart in the operator. Since the SM neutrinos are massless and purely left-handed, the only possibility is ∂μ(ν¯L​γμ​νL)\partial_{\mu}(\bar{\nu}_{L}\gamma^{\mu}\nu_{L}) with Lorentz indices fully contracted. Then, the equation of motion for a massless neutrino renders ∂μγμ​νL\partial_{\mu}\gamma^{\mu}\nu_{L} to vanish. Although constructing a Majorana mass term with only left-handed neutrinos is possible, lepton number is not violated in weak interactions and hence cannot appear without involving other new physics.

IV.0.2 The Vector Operator 𝒪e​ν​χV{\cal O}_{e\nu\chi}^{V}

For the vector operator, the 2-body χ→ν​γ\chi\to\nu\gamma and 3-body χ→ν​γ​γ\chi\to\nu\gamma\gamma channels cannot arise at 1-loop level. The vanishing of χ→ν​γ\chi\to\nu\gamma is due to the gauge symmetry. As mentioned in the previous paragraph, the electron current e¯​γμ​e\bar{e}\gamma_{\mu}e in the vector operator 𝒪e​ν​χV{\cal O}_{e\nu\chi}^{V} contributes to the loop mediator and needs to be integrated way with a remaining photon field as external state. This feature is generally parametrized as matrix element ⟨γ⁡(q,ϵ)|e¯​γμ​e|0⟩\langle\gamma(q,\epsilon)|\bar{e}\gamma_{\mu}e|0\rangle. In the presence of an external photon, the matrix element is a linear function of its polarization vector ϵμ∗\epsilon^{*}_{\mu}. Another quantity that can provide a Lorentz index is the momentum transfer qμq_{\mu}. The full matrix element also contains a piece u¯ν​γμ​PL​uχ\bar{u}_{\nu}\gamma^{\mu}P_{L}u_{\chi} from the neutrino side,

ℳ≡[A⁡(q2)​qμ​ϵ∗⋅q+B⁡(q2)​ϵμ∗]​(u¯ν​γμ​PL​uχ)≡ϵμ∗​ℳμ.\displaystyle\mathcal{M}\equiv\left[A(q^{2})q_{\mu}\epsilon^{*}\cdot q+B(q^{2})\epsilon_{\mu}^{*}\right](\bar{u}_{\nu}\gamma^{\mu}P_{L}u_{\chi})\equiv\epsilon_{\mu}^{*}{\cal M}^{\mu}. (22)

The coefficients A⁡(q2)A(q^{2}) and B⁡(q2)B(q^{2}) correlate with each other by the QED Ward identity: qμ​ℳμ=0q_{\mu}{\cal M}^{\mu}=0 from replacing the photon polarization vector ϵμ∗\epsilon^{*}_{\mu} with its four-momentum qμq_{\mu}. Namely,

[A⁡(q2)​q2+B⁡(q2)]​qμ​(u¯ν​γμ​PL​uχ)=0.\displaystyle\left[A(q^{2})q^{2}+B(q^{2})\right]q_{\mu}(\bar{u}_{\nu}\gamma^{\mu}P_{L}u_{\chi})=0. (23)

Since qμ≡pχμ−pνμq^{\mu}\equiv p_{\chi}^{\mu}-p_{\nu}^{\mu}, the second term qμ​(u¯ν​γμ​PL​uχ)=u¯ν​(p̸χ−p̸ν)​PL​uχ=mχ​ν¯ν​PR​uχ≠0q_{\mu}(\bar{u}_{\nu}\gamma^{\mu}P_{L}u_{\chi})=\bar{u}_{\nu}(\not{p}_{\chi}-\not{p}_{\nu})P_{L}u_{\chi}=m_{\chi}\bar{\nu}_{\nu}P_{R}u_{\chi}\neq 0 is nonzero. Then the only solution is B⁡(q2)=−A⁡(q2)​q2B(q^{2})=-A(q^{2})q^{2} and the effective current,

⟨γ⁡(q,ϵ)|e¯​γμ​e|0⟩=A⁡(q2)​(q2​ϵμ∗−qμ​ϵ∗⋅q),\displaystyle\langle\gamma(q,\epsilon)|\bar{e}\gamma_{\mu}e|0\rangle=A(q^{2})(q^{2}\epsilon^{*}_{\mu}-q_{\mu}\epsilon^{*}\cdot q), (24)

vanishes due to the photon on-shell (q2=0q^{2}=0) and transverse (ϵ∗⋅q=0\epsilon^{*}\cdot q=0) conditions. For the 2-photon decay χ→ν​γ​γ\chi\rightarrow\nu\gamma\gamma, the loop part again contains 3 currents and hence vanishes due to the QED charge conjugation symmetry.

The dominant visible decay channel is the 4-body process χ→ν​γ​γ​γ\chi\to\nu\gamma\gamma\gamma whose matrix elment can be generally parametrized as,

ℳν​γ​γ​γ=−e316​π2​Λ2​(u¯ν​γμ​PL​uχ)​ϵ1​α∗​ϵ2​β∗​ϵ3​ρ∗​Πμ​α​β​ρ,\displaystyle{\cal M}_{\nu\gamma\gamma\gamma}=-{e^{3}\over 16\pi^{2}\Lambda^{2}}(\bar{u}_{\nu}\gamma_{\mu}P_{L}u_{\chi})\epsilon_{1\alpha}^{*}\epsilon_{2\beta}^{*}\epsilon_{3\rho}^{*}\Pi^{\mu\alpha\beta\rho}, (25)

where ϵi∗\epsilon_{i}^{*} is the polarization vector of the ii-th final-state photon. The tensor Πμ​α​β​ρ\Pi^{\mu\alpha\beta\rho} is the reduced matrix element from the the electron loop in Fig. 5(c). Correspondingly, the spin averaged squared matrix amplitude becomes,

|ℳχ→ν​γ​γ​γ|2¯=16​α3π​Λ4​{−14​Tr​[p̸ν​γμ​p̸χ​γν]​(18​Πμ​α​β​ρ)​(18​Πα​β​ρν)}.\displaystyle\overline{|{\cal M}_{\chi\to\nu\gamma\gamma\gamma}|^{2}}={16\alpha^{3}\over\pi\Lambda^{4}}\left\{-{1\over 4}\mbox{Tr}\left[\not{p}_{\nu}\gamma_{\mu}\not{p}_{\chi}\gamma_{\nu}\right]\left({1\over 8}\Pi^{\mu\alpha\beta\rho}\right)\left({1\over 8}\Pi^{\nu}_{~\alpha\beta\rho}\right)\right\}. (26)

The reduced matrix element Πμ​α​β​ρ\Pi^{\mu\alpha\beta\rho} is evaluated first analytically by Package-X [128] and then numerically by COLLIER [129]. The decay width is an integral over the 4-body phase space d​Φ4d\Phi_{4},

Γχ→ν​γ​γ​γV=13!​12​mχ​∫d​Φ4​|ℳχ→ν​γ​γ​γ|2¯,\displaystyle\Gamma_{\chi\to\nu\gamma\gamma\gamma}^{V}={1\over 3!}{1\over 2m_{\chi}}\int d\Phi_{4}\overline{|{\cal M}_{\chi\to\nu\gamma\gamma\gamma}|^{2}}, (27)

with the factor 1/3!1/3! to avoid phase space overcounting for the 3 identical photons. In the limit of mχ≪2​mem_{\chi}\ll 2m_{e}, the decay width also has a simple scaling behavior,

Γχ→ν​γ​γ​γV≈2.6×10−29​sec−1​(mχ200​keV)13​(TeVΛ)4.\displaystyle\Gamma_{\chi\to\nu\gamma\gamma\gamma}^{V}\approx 2.6\times 10^{-29}{\rm sec^{-1}}\left(m_{\chi}\over 200\,\rm keV\right)^{13}\left(\rm TeV\over\Lambda\right)^{4}. (28)

For the DM invisible decay χ→3​ν\chi\to 3\nu, the loop diagrams (d) and (e) in Fig. 5 suffer from UV divergence. To make a reasonable estimation, we use the dimensional regularization (DR) to tackle this issue. For the WW-loop contribution, the amplitude in the unitary gauge is

ℳχ→3​νW=−u¯ν​γμ​PL​uχΛ2​3​g2264​π2​[1+me2mW2​(1ϵ+116+ln⁡Λ2mW2)+⋯]​[u¯νe​(p1)​γμ​PL​vνe​(p2)],\displaystyle{\cal M}_{\chi\to 3\nu}^{W}=-{\bar{u}_{\nu}\gamma^{\mu}P_{L}u_{\chi}\over\Lambda^{2}}{3g_{2}^{2}\over 64\pi^{2}}\left[1+{m_{e}^{2}\over m_{W}^{2}}\left({1\over\epsilon}+{11\over 6}+\ln{\Lambda^{2}\over m_{W}^{2}}\right)+\cdots\right]\left[\bar{u}_{\nu_{e}}(p_{1})\gamma_{\mu}P_{L}v_{\nu_{e}}(p_{2})\right], (29)

where g2g_{2} is the weak coupling constant while μ\mu the dimensional regularization scale. The terms in the bracket is from the WW-loop for generating the electron neutrino pair, and ⋯\cdots stand for terms suppressed by higher powers of q2/mW2q^{2}/m_{W}^{2}. Dropping the divergent piece 1/ϵ1/\epsilon altogether with the terms proportional to q2/mW2q^{2}/m_{W}^{2}, the finite amplitude used in our estimation is,

ℳχ→3​νW≈−1Λ2​3​g2264​π2​(u¯ν​γμ​PL​uχ)​[u¯νe​(p1)​γμ​PL​vνe​(p2)].\displaystyle{\cal M}_{\chi\to 3\nu}^{W}\approx-{1\over\Lambda^{2}}{3g_{2}^{2}\over 64\pi^{2}}(\bar{u}_{\nu}\gamma^{\mu}P_{L}u_{\chi})[\bar{u}_{\nu_{e}}(p_{1})\gamma_{\mu}P_{L}v_{\nu_{e}}(p_{2})]. (30)

The amplitude and decay width depend on the neutrino flavor that appears in the DM absorption operator. For (ν¯e​γμ​χL)(\bar{\nu}_{e}\gamma^{\mu}\chi_{L}), there are two diagrams by exchanging the two electron neutrinos but only a single one for (ν¯μ,τ​γμ​χL)(\bar{\nu}_{\mu,\tau}\gamma^{\mu}\chi_{L}). Considering this difference, the decay width for muon/tau flavor is,

Γχ→3​νV≈mχ51536​π3​(3​g2264​π2)2​1Λ4≈3.66×10−17​sec−1​(mχ200​keV)5​(TeVΛ)4,\displaystyle\Gamma_{\chi\to 3\nu}^{V}\approx{m_{\chi}^{5}\over 1536\pi^{3}}\left({3g_{2}^{2}\over 64\pi^{2}}\right)^{2}{1\over\Lambda^{4}}\approx 3.66\times 10^{-17}{\rm sec}^{-1}\left(m_{\chi}\over\rm 200~{\rm keV}\right)^{5}\left({\rm TeV}\over{\rm\Lambda}\right)^{4}, (31)

and for the electron neutrino in 𝒪e​ν​χV{\cal O}_{e\nu\chi}^{V}, there is an additional enhancement factor 2. Note that the ZZ boson mediated diagram of Fig. 5(e) is always suppressed by 1/mZ21/m^{2}_{Z} and hence can be neglected.

IV.0.3 The Axial-Vector Operator 𝒪e​ν​χA{\cal O}_{e\nu\chi}^{A}

The dominant decay modes for the axial-vector operator 𝒪e​ν​χA{\cal O}_{e\nu\chi}^{A} are the 3-body decay χ→ν​γ​γ\chi\to\nu\gamma\gamma and χ→3​ν\chi\to 3\nu. This is because the 2-body mode χ→ν​γ\chi\to\nu\gamma and the 4-body one χ→ν​γ​γ​γ\chi\to\nu\gamma\gamma\gamma with an odd number of photons in the final state are forbidden by the QED charge conjugation symmetry.

First, the 3-body process χ→ν​γ​γ\chi\to\nu\gamma\gamma is generated through the similar electron loop as the scalar and pseudo-scalar cases. The exact decay width is,

Γχ→ν​γ​γA=1Λ4​α2512​π5​me4​mχ​∫0mχ2d​s12​s122​(mχ2−s12)2​|FA​(η)|2,\displaystyle\Gamma_{\chi\to\nu\gamma\gamma}^{A}={1\over\Lambda^{4}}{\alpha^{2}\over 512\pi^{5}m_{e}^{4}m_{\chi}}\int_{0}^{m_{\chi}^{2}}ds_{12}s_{12}^{2}(m_{\chi}^{2}-s_{12})^{2}|F_{A}(\eta)|^{2}, (32)

where s12s_{12} is again the squared invariant mass of the two final-state photons and η≡s12/me2\eta\equiv s_{12}/m_{e}^{2}. The new loop function FA​(η)F_{A}(\eta),

FA​(η)≡−1η−1η2​ln2​η−4−ηη−4+η,\displaystyle F_{A}(\eta)\equiv-{1\over\eta}-{1\over\eta^{2}}\ln^{2}{\sqrt{\eta-4}-\sqrt{\eta}\over\sqrt{\eta-4}+\sqrt{\eta}}, (33)

reduces to FA​(η)≈1/12F_{A}(\eta)\approx 1/12 in the limit of mχ≪2​mem_{\chi}\ll 2m_{e}. Accordingly, the decay width scales as

Γχ→ν​γ​γA≈9×10−22​sec−1​(mχ200​keV)9​(TeVΛ)4,\displaystyle\Gamma_{\chi\to\nu\gamma\gamma}^{A}\approx 9\times 10^{-22}{\rm sec^{-1}}\left(m_{\chi}\over 200\,\rm keV\right)^{9}\left(\rm TeV\over\Lambda\right)^{4}, (34)

for tiny DM mass. Note that the dependence on mχm_{\chi} is higher by 2 powers than that of the scalar and pseudo-scalar cases in (21).

Second, the invisible decay χ→3​ν\chi\to 3\nu shares the similar features as that of the vector case including the divergence. We use the same procedure to keep only the leading non-divergent term,

Γχ→3​νA≈mχ51536​π3​(3​g2264​π2)2​1Λ4≈3.66×10−17​sec−1​(mχ200​keV)5​(TeVΛ)4.\displaystyle\Gamma_{\chi\to 3\nu}^{A}\approx{m_{\chi}^{5}\over 1536\pi^{3}}\left({3g_{2}^{2}\over 64\pi^{2}}\right)^{2}{1\over\Lambda^{4}}\approx 3.66\times 10^{-17}{\rm sec}^{-1}\left(m_{\chi}\over\rm 200~{\rm keV}\right)^{5}\left({\rm TeV}\over{\rm\Lambda}\right)^{4}. (35)

for the 𝒪e​ν​χA{\cal O}_{e\nu\chi}^{A} operator with a muon/tau neutrino. There is also an additional factor 2 for the electron neutrino case.

IV.0.4 The Tensor Operator 𝒪e​ν​χT{\cal O}_{e\nu\chi}^{T}

The dominant decay mode for the tensor operator is the 2-body decay χ→ν​γ\chi\to\nu\gamma in Fig. 5(a). However, it suffers from UV divergence,

ℳχ→ν​γ=1Λ2​(u¯ν​σμ​ν​PR​uχ)​[−i​e​me​qμ​ϵν∗2​π2​(1ϵ+ln⁡Λ2me2)],\displaystyle{\cal M}_{\chi\to\nu\gamma}={1\over\Lambda^{2}}(\bar{u}_{\nu}\sigma^{\mu\nu}P_{R}u_{\chi})\left[-i{em_{e}q_{\mu}\epsilon^{*}_{\nu}\over 2\pi^{2}}\left({1\over\epsilon}+\ln{\Lambda^{2}\over m_{e}^{2}}\right)\right], (36)

and needs to be regularized by the DR scheme. The vectors qμq_{\mu} and ϵν∗\epsilon_{\nu}^{*} are the outgoing photon momentum and polarization vector, respectively. After dropping the divergent factor 1/ϵ1/\epsilon, the decay width from the the finite part becomes

Γχ→ν​γT=α​me2​mχ316​π4​Λ4​ln2​Λ2me2≈1.5×10−8​sec−1​(mχ200​keV)3​(TeVΛ)4​ln2⁡(Λ2/me2)1000,\displaystyle\Gamma_{\chi\to\nu\gamma}^{T}={\alpha m_{e}^{2}m_{\chi}^{3}\over 16\pi^{4}\Lambda^{4}}\ln^{2}{\Lambda^{2}\over m_{e}^{2}}\approx 1.5\times 10^{-8}{\rm sec^{-1}}\left(m_{\chi}\over 200\,\rm keV\right)^{3}\left(\rm TeV\over\Lambda\right)^{4}{\ln^{2}(\Lambda^{2}/m_{e}^{2})\over 1000}, (37)

where the cut-off scale Λ\Lambda enters through the log term. Since the logarithm is not sensitive to the change of Λ\Lambda, we approximate it by a typical value ln2⁡(Λ2/me2)∼𝒪⁡(103)\ln^{2}(\Lambda^{2}/m_{e}^{2})\sim{\cal O}(10^{3}). Comparing (37) with (21), (28) and (34), we see that the χ→ν​γ\chi\to\nu\gamma decay width for 𝒪e​ν​χT{\cal O}_{e\nu\chi}^{T} is much larger than the dominant visible decay width for all other operators. This implies that a much stronger constraint will be put on the tensor operator. Again, the 3-body channel χ→ν​γ​γ\chi\to\nu\gamma\gamma vanishes due to the QED charge conjugation symmetry . In addition, the 4-body decay χ→ν​γ​γ​γ\chi\to\nu\gamma\gamma\gamma is suppressed by additional couplings as well as phase space factor.

For the invisible decay χ→3​ν\chi\to 3\nu, as dictated by Lorentz invariance and the left-handedness of SM neutrinos, the electron tensor structure (e¯​σμ​ν​e)(\bar{e}\sigma^{\mu\nu}e) induces an effective operator (me/mW2)​∂μ(ν¯L​γν​νL)(m_{e}/m_{W}^{2})\partial^{\mu}(\bar{\nu}_{L}\gamma^{\nu}\nu_{L}) after loop integration. The electron mass mem_{e} comes from the chirality flip introduced by the tensor operator. With the mass dimensions of mem_{e} and ∂μ\partial^{\mu} compensated by 1/mW21/m_{W}^{2}, this contribution is severely suppressed by a factor me2/mW2∼10−11m_{e}^{2}/m_{W}^{2}\sim 10^{-11} than χ→ν​γ\chi\to\nu\gamma and can be safely neglected.

V The cosmological and astrophysical constraints on DM Decays

As elaborated above, the DM absorption operators contain only one DM field. There is no intrinsic mechanism to forbid DM from decaying. This can provide some visible effect on the cosmological evolution history and the astrophysical observations via X-ray and gamma ray. This section evaluates first the constraints from cosmology in Sec. V.1 and astrophysical observations in Sec. V.2.

V.1 The Cosmological Evolution Constraints on the DM Invisible Decay χ→3​ν\chi\to 3\nu

As illustrated in Sec. IV, both the vector and axial-vector operators can have invisible decay χ→3​ν\chi\rightarrow 3\nu. More importantly, the invisible decay mode dominates over the visible ones by at least 4 orders. This can be seen by comparing (28) with (31), and (34) with (35). If a significant amount of the DM decays invisibly to inject its energy into relativistic degrees of freedom, the expansion history of the Universe can receive sizable modifications. Previous studies have already put quite strong constraints on the decaying DM scenario [130, 131, 132, 133]. The currently most stringent constraint is Γinv−1<468​Gyr\Gamma_{\rm inv}^{-1}<468\,\rm Gyr [134].

The constraints on σχ​eV,A​vχ\sigma_{\chi e}^{V,A}v_{\chi} are shown as dot-dashed lines in Fig. 4. The blue one is for the vector case while the magenta one for the axial-vector one. In the mass range 40​keV≲mχ≲500​keV40\,\rm keV\lesssim m_{\chi}\lesssim 500\,\rm keV, the constraints from χ→3​ν\chi\to 3\nu for the vector case is stronger than the DM overproduction and gamma-ray constraints. Together with the approximation σχ​e​vχ≈mχ2/4​π​Λ4\sigma_{\chi e}v_{\chi}\approx m^{2}_{\chi}/4\pi\Lambda^{4}, the scaling behaviors Γ3​νV,A∝mχ5/Λ4\Gamma^{V,A}_{3\nu}\propto m^{5}_{\chi}/\Lambda^{4} in (31) and (35) renders the constraint to scale as ∝1/mχ3\propto 1/m^{3}_{\chi}. This estimation is consistent with the resulting curves shown in Fig. 4. For other operators, the χ→3​ν\chi\rightarrow 3\nu channel is much smaller.

V.2 The Astrophysical X-Ray and Gamma Ray Constraints on the Visible Decays χ→ν+γ⁡(s)\chi\to\nu+\gamma(\rm s)

Although the visible decays are typically much smaller than the invisible one as explored in Sec. IV, it is much easier to observe photon than neutrino. This is especially true in the low energy range for sub-MeV DM. With DM distributing everywhere in the Universe and being especially concentrated in our Milky Way galaxy, the observation of diffuse X-ray and gamma ray can put stringent constraints on the decay width and therefore the cut-off scale Λ\Lambda. We first describe how the DM visible decays contribute to the X(gamma)-ray observations in Sec. V.2.1 and then compare with the astrophysics observation data sets in Sec. V.2.2.

V.2.1 X-Ray and Gamma Ray Fluxes from the Visible Decays

Both galactic and extra-galactic sources of DM visible decay χ→ν​γ​(s)\chi\rightarrow\nu\gamma(s) can contribute to the X(gamma)-ray observations around our Earth. Typically the extra-galactic contributions are much smaller than the galactic counterpart. But for those diffuse cosmic fluxes, the major contribution comes from extra-galactic sources. So we will discuss both contributions below.

For DM decay, the galactic contribution is proportional to its local density ρχ/mχ\rho_{\chi}/m_{\chi} and the decay spectrum d​Γχ/d​Eγd\Gamma_{\chi}/dE_{\gamma} calculated in the rest frame of DM. So the differential photon flux per unit energy per solid angle is,

d2​Φγd​Eγ​d​Ω=14​π​d​Γχd​Eγ​∫l.o.ssmaxρχ​(r)mχ​𝑑s,\displaystyle{d^{2}\Phi_{\gamma}\over dE_{\gamma}d\Omega}=\frac{1}{4\pi}\frac{d\Gamma_{\chi}}{dE_{\gamma}}\int^{s_{\rm max}}_{\rm l.o.s}\frac{\rho_{\chi}(r)}{m_{\chi}}ds, (38)

where d​Γχ/d​Eγd\Gamma_{\chi}/dE_{\gamma} is the corresponding differential decay width. The integration over the line of sight (l.o.s.) takes all the contribution along a specific direction. Note that the DM density ρχ​(r)\rho_{\chi}(r) is a direct function of the distance rr from the galactic center. We adopt the NFW profile, ρ⁡(r)=ρ0/[(r/rs)​(1+r/rs)2]\rho(r)=\rho_{0}/[(r/r_{s})(1+r/r_{s})^{2}] [135, 136], where rs=17r_{s}=17 kpc [137] and ρ0=0.43​GeV/cm3\rho_{0}=0.43\,\rm GeV/cm^{3} to give the local DM density ρχ≈0.4​GeV/cm3\rho_{\chi}\approx 0.4\,\rm GeV/cm^{3}. The distance r⁡(s)r(s) is a function of the l.o.s. distance ss in the galactic coordinate,

r⁡(s)=r⊙2+s2−2​r⊙​s​cos⁡ψ.\displaystyle r(s)=\sqrt{r_{\odot}^{2}+s^{2}-2r_{\odot}s\cos\psi}. (39)

In addition, r⊙=8.3​kpcr_{\odot}=8.3\,\rm kpc is the distance of Earth to the galactic center and cos⁡ψ≡cos⁡b​cos⁡l\cos\psi\equiv\cos b\cos l. The integration range for the l.o.s distance ss is from 0 to a maximal value determined by the virial radius rvir=300​kpcr_{\rm vir}=300\,\rm kpc of the DM halo [9],

smax=r⊙​cos⁡ψ+rvir2−r⊙2​sin2⁡ψ.\displaystyle s_{\rm max}=r_{\odot}\cos\psi+\sqrt{r_{\rm vir}^{2}-r_{\odot}^{2}\sin^{2}\psi}. (40)

The extra-galactic contribution comes from the smooth DM distribution in the whole universe. Its contribution is isotropic and integrated over a large range of the redshift [138],

d2​ΦrEGd​Eγ​d​Ω=ΩDM​ρc4​π​mχ​H0​Ωm​∫0∞d​Γχd​Eγ​(z)​d​zκ+(1+z)3.\displaystyle\frac{d^{2}\Phi_{r}^{\rm EG}}{dE_{\gamma}d\Omega}=\frac{\Omega_{\rm DM}\rho_{c}}{4\pi m_{\chi}H_{0}\sqrt{\Omega_{m}}}\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{d\Gamma_{\chi}}{dE_{\gamma}(z)}\frac{dz}{\sqrt{\kappa+(1+z)^{3}}}. (41)

The Hubble constant H0=67.4​km​sec−1​Mpc−1H_{0}=67.4\,\rm km\,sec^{-1}Mpc^{-1} and the cosmological critical density ρc=5.8×10−6​GeV​cm−3\rho_{c}=5.8\times 10^{-6}\,\rm GeV\,cm^{-3} are present values. Of the total matter fraction Ωm=0.315\Omega_{m}=0.315, DM takes the largest share ΩDM=0.265\Omega_{\rm DM}=0.265. In addition, the dark energy (DE) also has a large effect on the cosmological evolution, especially in the late stage. We use κ≡ΩΛ/Ωm=2.17\kappa\equiv{\Omega_{\Lambda}/\Omega_{m}}=2.17 to parametrize the contribution of DE. The decay width and spectrum calculated in Sec. IV cannot be used directly. Due to cosmological redshift, the photon energy Eγ​(z)=(1+z)​EγE_{\gamma}(z)=(1+z)E_{\gamma} emitted at redshift zz is 1+z1+z times of the apparent EγE_{\gamma}.

The total photon flux d2​Φr/d​Eγ​d​Ω{d^{2}\Phi_{r}/dE_{\gamma}d\Omega} due to DM decay is then a sum of the above two components. For a telescope with effective area AeffA_{\rm eff} and field of view (FOV) Δ​Ω\Delta\Omega as well as exposure time TobsT_{\rm obs}, the predicted photon event rate in energy bin [Ei−,Ei+][E^{-}_{i},E^{+}_{i}] is

Nith≡Aeff​Tobs​∫Ei−Ei+d​Eγ​∫Δ​Ωd​Ω​d2​Φγd​Eγ​d​Ω.\displaystyle N_{i}^{\rm th}\equiv A_{\rm eff}T_{\rm obs}\int_{E^{-}_{i}}^{E^{+}_{i}}dE_{\gamma}\int_{\Delta\Omega}d\Omega{d^{2}\Phi_{\gamma}\over dE_{\gamma}d\Omega}. (42)

Below we use real data to constrain the DM decay width and subsequently the DM coupling strength.

V.2.2 Constraints from Astrophysical X-ray and Gamma Ray Data in the keV-MeV Range

As argued at the beginning of Sec. II, we are interested in the DM mass range between keV and MeV. The relevant observations in our analysis include Insight-HXMT [139], NuSTAR [140, 141], HEAO-1 [142], and INTEGRAL [143, 144]. Fig. 6 summarizes the observed X(gamma)-ray data. Most data sets are used to constrain the fermionic DM absorption operators for the first time with the only exception of HEAO-1 and INTEGRAL-08 [138]. The constraints on the DM decay width Γχ\Gamma_{\chi} are shown in Fig. 7 while the constraints on the interaction strength in terms of the direct detection cross section σχ​e​vχ\sigma_{\chi e}v_{\chi} have already been included in Fig. 4 altogether.

To constrain the DM decay width Γχ\Gamma_{\chi}, we require the predicted photon events in each energy bin does not exceed the experimental counts at 95% C.L. In a single energy bin [Ei−,Ei+][E^{-}_{i},E^{+}_{i}], the constraint is obtained with

Nith≤Niobs≡Aeff​Tobs​Δ​Ω​(d2​Φγd​Eγ​d​Ω)exp​@​95%i​Δ​Ei.\displaystyle N_{i}^{\rm th}\leq N_{i}^{\rm obs}\equiv A_{\rm eff}T_{\rm obs}\Delta\Omega\left({d^{2}\Phi_{\gamma}\over dE_{\gamma}d\Omega}\right)_{\rm exp@95\%}^{i}\Delta E_{i}. (43)

In principle, one may directly compare the predicted flux d2​Φr/d​Eγ​d​Ωd^{2}\Phi_{r}/dE_{\gamma}d\Omega with the data in Fig. 6 without converting to event number in each bin. Nevertheless, the spectrum of the two-body channel χ→ν​γ\chi\rightarrow\nu\gamma for the tensor operator 𝒪e​ν​χT\mathcal{O}^{T}_{e\nu\chi} is a δ\delta function which is difficult to directly compare with Fig. 6. With multiple data points, we can obtain a corresponding limit for the decay width Γχi\Gamma_{\chi}^{i} from the ii-th energy bin, and we take the strongest bound among all bins as the final limit for the corresponding mass point.

Some data releases, especially Insight-HXMT [139] and NuSTAR/M31 [141], even provide background models in addition to data points. This opens the possibility to use χ2\chi^{2} fit to obtain enhanced sensitivity than simply comparing with the central value plus the 95% C.L. uncertainty for individual bins. Putting things together, the corresponding χ2\chi^{2} function for fitting the NuSTAR/M31 data is,

χ2​(xi,Λ)≡∑i[ΛTeV−4​NiDM​(Λ=1​TeV)+∑aca​Nia−Niexpδ​Ni]2,\displaystyle\chi^{2}(x_{i},\Lambda)\equiv\sum_{i}\left[\frac{\Lambda^{-4}_{\rm TeV}N_{i}^{\rm DM}({\Lambda=1\,\rm TeV})+\sum_{a}c_{a}N^{a}_{i}-N_{i}^{\rm exp}}{\delta N_{i}}\right]^{2}\!\!\!, (44)

where ΛTeV≡Λ/TeV\Lambda_{\rm TeV}\equiv\Lambda/\rm TeV. The observation data provides the central values NiexpN^{\rm exp}_{i} and the corresponding uncertainty δ​Ni\delta N_{i} for the ii-th bin. Each observation can have multiple backgrounds NiaN^{a}_{i} with aa denoting its type and cac_{a} the corresponding normalization factor. The χ2\chi^{2} fit with data takes cac_{a} as fitting parameters while the one for the DM contribution is the cut-off scale ΛTeV\Lambda_{\rm TeV} in unit of TeV. More details of the analytic χ2\chi^{2} fit can be found in App. A.

Below is a detailed description of each data set and their constraints on the DM decay width and coupling strength.

  • •

    Insight-HXMT/CXB: We use the (1∼12)(1\sim 12) keV cosmic X-ray background (CXB) data observed by the Low Energy X-ray Telescope on Insight-HXMT (Hard X-ray Modulation Telescope) [139]. The observation points to the sky in the direction (l,b)=(219.3∘,−50.0∘)(l,b)=(219.3^{\circ},-50.0^{\circ}) with a small FOV (1.6∘×6∘1.6^{\circ}\times 6^{\circ}). The relevant effective detector area is taken from the Fig. 1 on the HXMT website [145]. For comparison, the background model for CXB is taken from the yellow line of the Fig. 11 therein. With both data points and background model provided, we use analytic χ2\chi^{2} fit to obtain constraint. The result is shown in Fig. 7 with blue color. In the 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1) keV range, Insight-HXMT/CXB gives a strong constraint.

  • •

    NuSTAR/CXB: The Fig. 10 of [140] gives the average CXB spectrum within the 3∼203\sim 20 keV energy range. This spectrum is obtained by stacking the focal plane module (FPM) A and B (FPMA and FPMB) observations with all six data sets (COSMOS EP1,2,3, EGS, ECDFS, UDS).

  • •

    NuSTAR/M31: In addition to the diffuse CXB, galaxy observation can also provide a strong constraint due to the concentrated DM density profile. A typical case is the NuSTAR observation of M31. We use the (5∼100)(5\sim 100) keV data in the Fig. 2 of [141] from the observation ID 50026002003. The NuSTAR instrumental and solar contributions, the 0-bounce CXB component, and the 2-bounce component from the diffuse M31 emission are taken into consideration as backgrounds. The background models are taken from the fit curves in the Fig. 2 of [141]. Each component has its own normalization factor as fitting parameter. Since the 2-bounce CXB component is very small, we neglect it in our χ2\chi^{2} fit to avoid numerical instability.

    For the DM decay photons, the 0-bounce and 2-bounce DM decay photons have different effective areas. To properly take the 2-bounce contribution into account, we use the enhancement factor defined in [141],

    ξ⁡(Eγ)≡1+A2​b​(Eγ)​Δ​Ω2​b​𝒥2​bA0​b​Δ​Ω0​b​𝒥0​b.\displaystyle\xi(E_{\gamma})\equiv 1+\frac{A_{\rm 2b}(E_{\gamma})\Delta\Omega_{\rm 2b}{\cal J}_{\rm 2b}}{A_{\rm 0b}\Delta\Omega_{\rm 0b}{\cal J}_{\rm 0b}}. (45)

    Then the predicted DM decay photon events in each energy bin can be written as,

    NiDM≡A0​b​Tobs​Δ​Ω0​b​𝒥0​b4​π​mχ​∫d​Eγ​ξ​(Eγ)​d​Γγd​Eγ,\displaystyle N_{i}^{\rm DM}\equiv A_{\rm 0b}T_{\rm obs}\Delta\Omega_{\rm 0b}\frac{\mathcal{J}_{\rm 0b}}{4\pi m_{\chi}}\int dE_{\gamma}\xi(E_{\gamma}){d\Gamma_{\gamma}\over dE_{\gamma}}, (46)

    where the observational effective area for the 0-bounce photons is A0​b=11.85​(11.80)​cm2A_{0b}=11.85\,(11.80)\,\rm cm^{2}, the exposure time is Tobs=82.4​(82.2)​ksT_{\rm obs}=82.4\,(82.2)\,\rm ks and the FOV Δ​Ω0​b=4.45​(4.55)​deg2\Delta\Omega_{0b}=4.45\,(4.55)\,\rm deg^{2} for the FPMA (FPMB) observation, respectively. The DM decay factor 𝒥0​b=6.72​(7.13)​GeV​cm−3​kpc​sr−1{\cal J}_{\rm 0b}=6.72\,(7.13)\,\rm GeV\,cm^{-3}\,kpc\,sr^{-1} for FPMA (FPMB) includes both the Milky Way and M31 contributions. One can neglect the extragalactic contribution which is much smaller.

  • •

    HEOA-1: The HEAO-1 extragalactic diffuse X-ray data in the Fig. 2 of [142] corresponds to the sky region l∈(58∘,106∘)∪(238∘,289∘),|b|∈(20∘,90∘)l\in(58^{\circ},106^{\circ})\cup(238^{\circ},289^{\circ}),|b|\in(20^{\circ},90^{\circ}). Following [138], we only use the (3∼50)(3\sim 50) keV data set observed by the A2 High-Energy Detector (HED).

  • •

    INTEGRAL: We use both the galactic center gamma-ray spectrum (|b|<15∘|b|<15^{\circ} and |l|<30∘|l|<30^{\circ}) as well as the galactic ridge emission spectrum from the SPI measurements on board INTEGRAL. 1) There are two data sets for the galactic center gamma-ray spectrum with photon energy (20∼2000)(20\sim 2000) keV. One is from the Fig. 9 of [143] released in 2008 and shown as INTEGRAL/08 (magenta) in Fig. 6 while the other comes from the Fig. 6 of [144] released in 2011 and shown as INTEGRAL/11C (yellow). 2) For the galactic ridge emission spectrum, the Fig. 4 of [144] gives the diffuse emission as a function of galactic longitude with the latitude being integrated over and the Fig. 5 therein gives the one with the longitude being integrated over. The INTEGRAL measurements from this analysis are divided into five energy bins with divisions at E=(27,49,100,200,600,1800)E=(27,49,100,200,600,1800) keV, respectively. We select those bins that give the strongest limit and show their corresponding fluxes in Fig. 6 as INTEGRAL/11R (black).

Fig. 7 compiles all the astrophysical X-ray and gamma-ray constraints on the DM visible decay. While the photon energy is typically smaller than half of the DM mass, Eγ<mχ/2E_{\gamma}<m_{\chi}/2, the energy range (1∼3000)(1\sim 3000) keV in Fig. 6 covers the DM mass window (2∼1000)(2\sim 1000) keV in Fig. 7. Although there are three different decay channels, χ→(ν​γ,ν​γ​γ,ν​γ​γ​γ)\chi\rightarrow(\nu\gamma,\nu\gamma\gamma,\nu\gamma\gamma\gamma), the last two share similar features of continum spectrum while the first has a discrete δ\delta function. For illustration purpose, we only show the vector and tensor cases in the left and right panels of Fig. 7, respectively. Due to this difference, the curves for the vector case are quite smooth while the tensor ones have many breaks and spikes. In addition, the tensor case typically has much clearer boundaries such as the NuSTAR/M31 curve. The results for χ→ν​γ​γ\chi\rightarrow\nu\gamma\gamma are quite similar to those of χ→ν​γ​γ​γ\chi\rightarrow\nu\gamma\gamma\gamma.

It is interesting to observe that, although the NuSTAR/M31 flux in Fig. 6 is not as small as other observations, its constraint on the DM visible decay width is not bad and even better than some others such as INTEGRAL. This is because the INTEGRAL constraints comes from comparing the theoretical prediction with all observed event counts plus errors at 95% C.L. while the NuSTAR/M31 constraint is comes from a more realistic χ2\chi^{2} fit. If possible, χ2\chi^{2} fit is more desirable although doing this for all astrophysical data is beyond the scope of the current paper.

Another important feature is that, the constraining power can go beyond the Eγ<mχ/2E_{\gamma}<m_{\chi}/2 correspondence. Taking the Insight-HXMT curve for demonstration, the adopted spectrum spans the energy range (1∼12)(1\sim 12) keV while the constrained mass range can extend up to 𝒪⁡(100)\mathcal{O}(100) keV. This is because the extragalactic contributions from the vast Universe receive redshift to different extent. Although the emitted photon spectrum is fixed by the DM mass mχm_{\chi} and the decay vertex, the observed photon energy could be much lower. A heavier mχm_{\chi} above the energy window can also receive constraint from low energy X-ray observation.

The constraints in terms of the direct detection cros section σχ​e​vχ\sigma_{\chi e}v_{\chi} have already been shown in Fig. 4 for comparison. Comparing with the overproduction constraints, the decay constraints are typically more stringent for heavier DM for both the invisible and visible channels. This is because the decay width typically grows with the DM mass. The constraint for the tensor operator is particularly strong since it comes from the single photon channel χ→ν​γ\chi\rightarrow\nu\gamma with much larger phase space. The next highly constrained operator is the pseudo-scalar type. Neither the freeze-in production nor decay process of the pseudo-scalar operator is suppressed for the others. So the constraints on its cut-off scale should be roughly the same as others. However, the direct detection cross section is highly suppressed for the pseudo-scalar case. Both pseudo-scalar and tensor operators are difficult to be directly probed. The constraints on the other operators are not that severe. Of them, the vector case is of particular interest for tonne-scale direct detection experiments (such as PandaX-4T [146, 147], XENONnT [148], and LZ [149, 150]) which will soon be able to probe small DM mass mχm_{\chi} of 𝒪⁡(10∼100)\mathcal{O}(10\sim 100) keV that has not been excluded by cosmological or astrophysical constraints.

VI Conclusions

We systematically investigated the fermionic DM absorption on the electron target that allow unique probe of sub-MeV DM. Using the effective fermionic absorption operators, we found that the electron recoil spectrum in direct detection has roughly the same shape that is mainly determined by the atomic KK-factor for different operators. This allows a model-independent, or at least operator-independent, measurement to some extent. It even allows in-situ measurement of the atomic KK-factor if the fermionic DM absorption is confirmed. The only complication is that the pseudo-scalar case has quite different signal size. The comparison with the Xenon1T and PandaX-II electron recoil spectrum prefers a vector-type DM absorption with mχ=59m_{\chi}=59 keV and 105 keV respectively. With the corresponding best-fit value Λ≈1\Lambda\approx 1 TeV, the Xenon1T and PandaX-II can probe the new physics cut-off scale up to TeV scale. We also systematically update the overproduction, cosmological, and astrophysical constraints. Especially, the X(gamma)-ray constraints from the Insight-HXMT, NuSTAR, and INTEGRAL 2011 data sets are newly used to constrain the sub-MeV fermionic absorption DM. Even though the tensor and pseudo-scalar operators are strongly constrained, the fermionic DM absorption with other operator types is still testable at tonne-scale experiments.

Appendix A Analytic χ2\chi^{2} Fit with Collective Marginalization

The fitting with experimental data points in this paper is achieved with analytical χ2\chi^{2} fit [113, 114]. With Gaussian distribution, the χ2\chi^{2} minimization is equivalent to matrix manipulation. Most importantly, the marginalization for a single parameter can also be done as matrix element manipulation to reduce a χ2\chi^{2} function with nn parameters to the one with n−1n-1 parameters. This single-parameter marginalization needs to be done recursively in order to marginalize over multiple parameters. Here we provide a more elegant formalism to marginalize over multiple parameters collectively.

Given a set of observables 𝒪j{\cal O}_{j}, the χ2\chi^{2} function can be generally parametrized as,

χ2=∑j(𝒪jth−𝒪jexpΔ​𝒪j)2,\displaystyle\chi^{2}=\sum_{j}\left({{\cal O}_{j}^{\rm th}-{\cal O}_{j}^{\rm exp}\over\Delta{\cal O}_{j}}\right)^{2}, (47)

where 𝒪jth{\cal O}_{j}^{\rm th} and 𝒪jexp{\cal O}_{j}^{\rm exp} are the theoretical prediction and experimental observation for the jj-th bin, respectively. A Gaussian χ2\chi^{2} function is equivalent to linear dependence of 𝒪jth{\cal O}_{j}^{\rm th} on the model parameters xi,(i=1,2,…,n)x_{i},(i=1,2,...,n) as 𝒪jth≈𝒪jth,0+∑iAj​i​xi{\cal O}_{j}^{\rm th}\approx\mathcal{O}^{\rm th,0}_{j}+\sum_{i}A_{ji}x_{i}. In matrix form, the χ2\chi^{2} function can be written as

χ2​(xi)=(𝒪th,0+A​x−𝒪exp)T​Σ¯−1​(𝒪th,0+A​x−𝒪exp),Σ¯−1≡diag⁡(Δ​𝒪j−2).\displaystyle\chi^{2}(x_{i})=(\mathcal{O}^{\rm th,0}+Ax-{\cal O}^{\rm exp})^{\rm T}\overline{\Sigma}^{-1}(\mathcal{O}^{\rm th,0}+Ax-{\cal O}^{\rm exp}),\quad\overline{\Sigma}^{-1}\equiv{\rm diag}(\Delta{\cal O}_{j}^{-2}). (48)

For mm observales and nn fitting parameters, AA is a m×nm\times n constant coefficient matrix and x≡(x1,⋯,xn)Tx\equiv(x_{1},\cdots,x_{n})^{T} is a n×1n\times 1 column vector. Then AA converts the n×1n\times 1 parameter vector xx to a m×1m\times 1 observable vector A​xAx that can match with 𝒪th,0\mathcal{O}^{\rm th,0} and 𝒪exp\mathcal{O}^{\rm exp}. Finally, the m×mm\times m error matrix Σ¯−1\overline{\Sigma}^{-1} in the observable space contracts with two observable vectors, one column and one row vectors, to produce a scalar χ2\chi^{2} function. By definition, error matrix is symmetric.

The χ2\chi^{2} minimization condition ∂χ2/∂xi≡0\partial\chi^{2}/\partial x_{i}\equiv 0 gives a unique solution for the best fit value of the fitting parameters,

xbest≡(AT​Σ¯−1​A)−1​AT​Σ¯−1​(𝒪th,0−𝒪exp).\displaystyle x_{\rm best}\equiv(A^{T}\overline{\Sigma}^{-1}A)^{-1}A^{T}\overline{\Sigma}^{-1}(\mathcal{O}^{\rm th,0}-{\cal O}^{\rm exp}). (49)

With larger deviation between the experimentally observed 𝒪exp\mathcal{O}^{\rm exp} and the zeroth-order prediction 𝒪th,0\mathcal{O}^{\rm th,0}, the fitting parameter should also deviate more from the one used to predict 𝒪th,0\mathcal{O}^{\rm th,0}. Correspondingly, the χ2\chi^{2} function splits into two parts

χ2​(xi)=χmin2+(x−xbest)T​Σ−1​(x−xbest),\displaystyle\chi^{2}(x_{i})=\chi^{2}_{\rm min}+(x-x_{\rm best})^{T}\Sigma^{-1}(x-x_{\rm best}), (50)

Now χ2\chi^{2} becomes a function of fitting parameters xix_{i}, instead of observables, with the corresponding n×nn\times n error matrix Σ−1≡AT​Σ¯−1​A\Sigma^{-1}\equiv A^{T}\overline{\Sigma}^{-1}A in the parameter space. The first term of (50) is the minimum value of the χ2\chi^{2},

χmin2≡(𝒪th,0−𝒪exp)T​BT​Σ¯−1​B​(𝒪th,0−𝒪exp)T,B≡𝕀−A​(AT​Σ¯−1​A)−1​AT​Σ¯−1,\displaystyle\chi^{2}_{\rm min}\equiv(\mathcal{O}^{\rm th,0}-{\cal O}^{\rm exp})^{T}B^{\rm T}\overline{\Sigma}^{-1}B(\mathcal{O}^{\rm th,0}-{\cal O}^{\rm exp})^{T},\quad B\equiv\mathbb{I}-A(A^{T}\overline{\Sigma}^{-1}A)^{-1}A^{T}\overline{\Sigma}^{-1}, (51)

while the second is actually δ​χ2​(xi)\delta\chi^{2}(x_{i}) as deviation from χmin2\chi^{2}_{\rm min}.

With multiple fitting parameters in (50), it is difficult to see the probability distribution of any specific one. It is desirable to obtain the χ2\chi^{2} of a single parameter by marginalizing over the others. This can be achieved by integrating out the unnecessary ones from the distribution function ℙ(x1,⋯xn)\mathbb{P}(x_{1},\cdots x_{n}). Taking one-parameter reduction for illustration,

ℙ⁡(x1,⋯,x^k,⋯,xn)=∫ℙ⁡(x1,⋯,xn)​d​xk,\displaystyle\mathbb{P}(x_{1},\cdots,\hat{x}_{k},\cdots,x_{n})=\int\mathbb{P}(x_{1},\cdots,x_{n})dx_{k}, (52)

where the kk-th element is marginalized. For a Gaussian distribution, this is equivalent to matrix element manipulation of the error matrix Σ−1\Sigma^{-1} in the parameter space,

Σ~i​j−1=Σi​j−1−Σi​k−1​Σj​k−1Σk​k−1.\displaystyle\widetilde{\Sigma}^{-1}_{ij}=\Sigma^{-1}_{ij}-\frac{\Sigma^{-1}_{ik}\Sigma^{-1}_{jk}}{\Sigma^{-1}_{kk}}. (53)

While Σ−1\Sigma^{-1} being a n×nn\times n matrix, Σ~−1\widetilde{\Sigma}^{-1} is (n−1)×(n−1)(n-1)\times(n-1) after marginalizing one single parameter xkx_{k}. Keeping doing this repeatedly, one can finally arrive at a χ2\chi^{2} function with only one parameter.

Nevertheless, this procedure is a little bit troublesome with n−1n-1 repetition when nn becomes large. Below we provide a more convenient algorithm of collective marginalization which can reduce a nn-parameter χ2\chi^{2} function directly to a single-parameter one without repetition. Suppose one needs to marginalize over kk parameters out of the original nn ones. Instead of using a single n×1n\times 1 vector xx, the fitting parameters can be separated into one (n−k)×1(n-k)\times 1 vector XX that shall remain and one k×1k\times 1 vector YY that needs to be marginalized away. Correspondingly, the experimental observables is predicted as

𝒪th,0+AX​X+AY​Y,\displaystyle\mathcal{O}^{\rm th,0}+A_{X}X+A_{Y}Y, (54)

instead of the original 𝒪th,0+A​x\mathcal{O}^{\rm th,0}+Ax. The χ2\chi^{2} function (48) then becomes

χ2​(X,Y)=(𝒪th,0+AX​X+AY​Y−𝒪exp)T​Σ¯−1​(𝒪th,0+AX​X+AY​Y−𝒪exp).\displaystyle\chi^{2}(X,Y)=(\mathcal{O}^{\rm th,0}+A_{X}X+A_{Y}Y-{\cal O}^{\rm exp})^{T}\overline{\Sigma}^{-1}(\mathcal{O}^{\rm th,0}+A_{X}X+A_{Y}Y-{\cal O}^{\rm exp}). (55)

For convenience, one may define δ​𝒪X≡𝒪th,0+AX​X−𝒪exp\delta\mathcal{O}_{X}\equiv\mathcal{O}^{\rm th,0}+A_{X}X-\mathcal{O}^{\rm exp} and the χ2​(X,Y)\chi^{2}(X,Y) function becomes,

χ2​(X,Y)=YT​ΣY−1​Y+2​YT​AYT​Σ¯−1​δ​𝒪X+δ​𝒪XT​Σ¯−1​δ​𝒪X,\displaystyle\chi^{2}(X,Y)=Y^{T}\Sigma^{-1}_{Y}Y+2Y^{T}A^{T}_{Y}\overline{\Sigma}^{-1}\delta\mathcal{O}_{X}+\delta\mathcal{O}^{T}_{X}\overline{\Sigma}^{-1}\delta\mathcal{O}_{X}, (56)

with ΣY−1≡AYT​Σ¯−1​AY\Sigma^{-1}_{Y}\equiv A^{T}_{Y}\overline{\Sigma}^{-1}A_{Y}. Only the first two terms are relevant in the Gaussian integration of the marginalization of YY,

ℙ⁡(X)=∫ℙ⁡(X,Y)​𝑑Y=N​∫e−12​χ2​(X,Y)​𝑑Y,\displaystyle\mathbb{P}(X)=\int\mathbb{P}(X,Y)dY=N\int e^{-\frac{1}{2}\chi^{2}(X,Y)}dY, (57)

with a normalization factor NN that would not affect the probability distribution. The result would be more transparent by reforming (56) as,

χ2​(X,Y)\displaystyle\chi^{2}(X,Y) =\displaystyle= (Y+ΣY​AYT​Σ¯−1​δ​𝒪X)T​ΣY−1​(Y+ΣY​AYT​Σ¯−1​δ​𝒪X)\displaystyle(Y+\Sigma_{Y}A^{T}_{Y}\overline{\Sigma}^{-1}\delta\mathcal{O}_{X})^{T}\Sigma^{-1}_{Y}(Y+\Sigma_{Y}A^{T}_{Y}\overline{\Sigma}^{-1}\delta\mathcal{O}_{X}) (58)
+\displaystyle+ δ​𝒪XT​[Σ¯−1−Σ¯−1​AY​ΣY​AYT​Σ¯−1]​δ​𝒪X.\displaystyle\delta\mathcal{O}^{T}_{X}\left[\overline{\Sigma}^{-1}-\overline{\Sigma}^{-1}A_{Y}\Sigma_{Y}A^{T}_{Y}\overline{\Sigma}^{-1}\right]\delta\mathcal{O}_{X}.

The first line is a Gaussian form of YY while the second line is independent of YY. Then the Gaussian integration (57) gives,

ℙ⁡(X)∝exp⁡[−12​(𝒪th,0+AX​X−𝒪exp)T​Σ¯X−1​(𝒪th,0+AX​X−𝒪exp)],\displaystyle\mathbb{P}(X)\propto\exp\left[-\frac{1}{2}(\mathcal{O}^{\rm th,0}+A_{X}X-{\cal O}^{\rm exp})^{T}\overline{\Sigma}^{-1}_{X}(\mathcal{O}^{\rm th,0}+A_{X}X-{\cal O}^{\rm exp})\right], (59)

up to a normalization factor. Since a Gaussian probability distribution is defined as ℙ(X)∝e−χ2(X)/2\mathbb{P}(X)\propto e^{-\chi^{2}(X)/2}, one can read off the reduced χ2​(X)\chi^{2}(X) directly from the above equation. The reduced experimental error matrix,

Σ¯X−1≡Σ¯−1−Σ¯−1​AY​ΣY​AYT​Σ¯−1,\displaystyle\overline{\Sigma}^{-1}_{X}\equiv\overline{\Sigma}^{-1}-\overline{\Sigma}^{-1}A_{Y}\Sigma_{Y}A^{T}_{Y}\overline{\Sigma}^{-1}, (60)

with only parameters XX replaces the original Σ¯−1\overline{\Sigma}^{-1}. It is interesting to observe that the reduced χ2​(X)\chi^{2}(X) in (59) resembles the original form (48). The effect of YY parameters is wholely encoded in Σ¯X−1\overline{\Sigma}^{-1}_{X}. It not only affects the XX error matrix, ΣX−1≡AXT​Σ¯X−1​AX\Sigma^{-1}_{X}\equiv A^{T}_{X}\overline{\Sigma}^{-1}_{X}A_{X}, but also its best fit values. The marginalization down to a single parameter corresponds to k=n−1k=n-1.
